title: From exact balance to a whole range

board_content.text: Equation vs. Inequality
An equation demands exact balance — one weight makes the scale rest level.
An inequality asks only: which side is heavier? It wants every value that tips it.
An equation's answer is a POINT. An inequality's answer is an INTERVAL.
Real life is full of them: luggage $w \le 15$ kg, pass marks $m \ge 33$, voting age $\ge 18$.
Each describes a whole band of acceptable values — that band is what we compute.

segments_english.text: <curious>Let me ask you something.</curious> For years now, what has an equation really been asking of you? Take a simple one.
Two x plus one equals seven. This is a demand for exact balance. Picture a weighing scale at the sabzi mandi, and there is exactly one weight, x equals three, that makes it rest perfectly level.
That single number is your whole answer — a point, one spot on the number line.
Now watch what changes when we drop the demand for balance. Two x plus one is greater than seven.
This does not want the value that balances the scale. It wants every single value that tips it to the heavier side.
And this is the biggest mental shift in the whole chapter. An equation's answer is a point; an inequality's answer is an interval, a whole stretch of the line.
Inequalities are everywhere. Your luggage must weigh at most fifteen kilograms. You need at least thirty three marks to pass. You must be eighteen or older to vote.
None of these is a single number. Each one describes a whole band of acceptable values, and computing that band is exactly what this subtopic teaches you.

segments_hinglish.text: <curious>एक बात सोचो।</curious> अब तक equation तुमसे असल में माँगता क्या था? एक simple सा example लो।
Two x plus one equals seven — ये exact balance की demand है। सोचो sabzi mandi का तराज़ू, और सिर्फ़ एक ही weight है, x equals three, जो उसे बिलकुल level पर रोक देता है।
वो एक number ही तुम्हारा पूरा answer है — एक point, number line पर बस एक जगह।
अब देखो क्या बदलता है जब हम balance वाली demand हटा देते हैं। Two x plus one is greater than seven।
अब इसे वो value नहीं चाहिए जो scale को balance करे — इसे हर वो value चाहिए जो उसे heavier side पर झुका दे।
और यही इस पूरे chapter का सबसे बड़ा mental shift है — equation का answer एक point होता है, पर inequality का answer एक interval, यानी line का एक पूरा हिस्सा।
Inequalities हर जगह हैं। Luggage at most fifteen kilograms का हो, pass होने के लिए at least thirty three marks चाहिए, vote करने के लिए eighteen या उससे ज़्यादा उम्र।
इनमें से कोई भी single number नहीं है — हर एक acceptable values का एक पूरा band बताता है, और वही band निकालना इस subtopic का काम है।

title: Marking the line, and the reflection that flips the sign

board_content.text: Painting the solution on the number line
A hollow circle means: get infinitely close, but this exact point is excluded — strict < or >.
A filled circle means: this endpoint is included too — non-strict $\le$ or $\ge$.

board_content.text: The one rule that makes inequalities different
Multiply or divide by a NEGATIVE ⇒ the sign flips.

segments_english.text: Once we have solved an inequality, the answer is a stretch of the number line — so we need a clean way to paint that stretch and mark its edges.
A hollow circle at the edge means: you may get infinitely close to this milestone, but this exact point is not allowed. That is what a strict less-than or greater-than looks like.
A filled circle means the opposite — this endpoint is allowed too. That marks a non-strict, less-than-or-equal or greater-than-or-equal.
Look at the two lines here. The top one, x greater than two, opens with a hollow circle at two. The bottom, x greater than or equal to two, fills that circle in. Same direction, different edge.
Now the one rule that truly separates inequalities from equations — and the source of more lost marks than any other idea in this chapter.
Start with negative two is less than three, which is true. Multiply both sides by negative one and you get two is greater than negative three. The symbol reversed.
So any time you multiply or divide by a negative number, the direction of the sign flips. Hold on to that.
Here is why, in a picture. Multiplying by negative one reflects every point across zero, and a reflection swaps left and right — so smaller and larger simply trade places.

segments_hinglish.text: एक बार inequality solve हो जाए, तो answer number line का एक हिस्सा होता है — इसलिए हमें उस हिस्से को mark करने का साफ़ तरीका चाहिए।
Edge पर hollow circle का मतलब है — तुम इस milestone के infinitely close तक जा सकते हो, पर ये exact point allowed नहीं है। यही strict less-than या greater-than दिखता है।
Filled circle इसका उल्टा है — ये endpoint भी allowed है। ये non-strict, यानी less-than-or-equal या greater-than-or-equal को mark करता है।
ये दो lines देखो। ऊपर वाली, x greater than two, two पर hollow circle से खुलती है। नीचे वाली, x greater than or equal to two, उसी circle को भर देती है। Direction same, edge अलग।
अब वो एक rule जो inequalities को equations से सचमुच अलग करता है — और इस chapter में सबसे ज़्यादा marks यहीं कटते हैं।
शुरू करो negative two is less than three से, जो सही है। दोनों sides को negative one से multiply करो, तो मिलता है two is greater than negative three। Symbol उल्टा हो गया।
तो जब भी तुम किसी negative number से multiply या divide करो, sign की direction flip हो जाती है। इसे पकड़ के रखो।
और ये रहा इसका picture। Negative one से multiply करना हर point को zero के across reflect कर देता है, और reflection left और right को swap कर देता है — इसलिए smaller और larger अपनी जगह बदल लेते हैं।

title: What counts as 'linear', and which moves are safe

board_content.text: Definitions
Linking two real expressions by <, >, $\le$, $\ge$ gives an inequality. < > are strict; $\le$ $\ge$ are non-strict (slack).
The set of all values that make it true is the solution set.
'Linear' = the variable appears only to the first power. No $x^2$, no $1/x$, no $|x|$.
Safe moves vs. the danger move
Add or subtract any quantity from both sides — always safe.
Multiply/divide by a POSITIVE number — safe. By a NEGATIVE — flip the sign.
Never cross-multiply by an unknown-sign expression like $x+3$. Never square unless both sides are $\ge 0$.

segments_english.text: Let us pin down the vocabulary, because the exam rewards precise language.

Any statement that links two real expressions by less-than, greater-than, less-than-or-equal, or greater-than-or-equal is an inequality. With less-than or greater-than it is strict; with the or-equal versions it is non-strict, sometimes called slack.
The set of every value that makes the statement true is called the solution set — and that set, written as an interval, is your final answer.
Now, linear has a precise meaning here. The variable may appear only to the first power. No x squared, no one-over-x, no modulus of x, unless that modulus can be unwound into linear pieces.
Within those guardrails, some moves are completely safe and one is dangerous.
You may add or subtract any quantity from both sides freely — addition never disturbs the direction of an inequality.
You may multiply or divide by a positive number freely. But multiply or divide by a negative number, and you must flip the sign.

<whisper>And two moves are simply forbidden.</whisper> Never cross-multiply by an expression whose sign you do not know, like x plus three, and never square both sides unless you are certain both are non-negative.

segments_hinglish.text: पहले vocabulary पक्की कर लें, क्योंकि exam precise language पर marks देता है।

कोई भी statement जो दो real expressions को less-than, greater-than, less-than-or-equal, या greater-than-or-equal से जोड़े, वो एक inequality है। Less-than या greater-than के साथ ये strict है; or-equal वाले versions के साथ non-strict, यानी slack।
हर वो value जो statement को true बनाए, उनका set कहलाता है solution set — और वही set, interval में लिखा हुआ, तुम्हारा final answer है।
अब, linear का यहाँ precise मतलब है। Variable सिर्फ़ first power में आ सकता है। ना x squared, ना one-over-x, ना modulus of x — जब तक कि वो modulus linear pieces में ना खुल जाए।
इन guardrails के अंदर, कुछ moves बिलकुल safe हैं और एक dangerous है।
तुम दोनों sides से कोई भी quantity add या subtract कर सकते हो — addition inequality की direction को कभी नहीं बिगाड़ता।
तुम किसी positive number से freely multiply या divide कर सकते हो। पर negative number से multiply या divide करो, तो sign flip करना ज़रूरी है।

<whisper>और दो moves बिलकुल forbidden हैं।</whisper> जिस expression का sign पता नहीं, जैसे x plus three, उससे कभी cross-multiply मत करो, और दोनों sides को तब तक square मत करो जब तक तुम्हें यक़ीन ना हो कि दोनों non-negative हैं।

title: The seven-step solving algorithm

board_content.text: How to solve any linear inequality
1. Clear fractions — multiply every term by the LCM of the denominators.
An LCM of positive integers is positive, so no flip occurs at this step.
2. Remove brackets. 3. Collect variable terms one side, constants the other — using only + and −.
5. Divide by $a$ — the ONLY dangerous step. If $a < 0$, reverse the symbol.
6. Write the solution set in interval notation.
7. Represent on a number line — hollow circles for < >, filled for $\le$ $\ge$.

segments_english.text: A linear inequality in one variable has no single derivation — it has an algorithm, and knowing why each step is safe is what stops the marks from leaking away.
Step one: clear all fractions by multiplying every term by the L C M of the denominators.
And here is why that is safe: an L C M of positive integers is itself positive, so by the order axioms no flip happens. Free of charge.

Step two, remove the brackets by distributing. Step three, collect the variable terms on one side and the constants on the other, using only addition and subtraction — and since adding never disturbs the direction, this whole stage is risk-free.
Step four leaves you in the clean form a x, sign, b.

Step five is the only dangerous move in the entire procedure. You divide by the coefficient a — and if a is negative, you must reverse the symbol. This is where careful students separate from careless ones.
Step six: write the solution set in interval notation.
And step seven: represent it on a number line, choosing hollow circles for strict less-than or greater-than, and filled circles for the or-equal versions.

segments_hinglish.text: एक-variable की linear inequality का कोई single derivation नहीं होता — इसका एक algorithm होता है, और हर step क्यों safe है ये जानना ही marks को बचाता है।
Step one — सारी fractions clear करो, हर term को denominators के L C M से multiply करके।
और ये safe क्यों है — positive integers का L C M खुद positive होता है, तो order axioms के हिसाब से कोई flip नहीं होता। बिलकुल मुफ़्त।

Step two, distribute करके brackets हटाओ। Step three, variable terms एक तरफ़ और constants दूसरी तरफ़ करो, सिर्फ़ addition और subtraction से — और चूँकि adding direction को नहीं बिगाड़ता, ये पूरा stage risk-free है।
Step four तुम्हें साफ़ form में छोड़ता है — a x, sign, b।
Step five पूरी procedure का एकमात्र dangerous move है। तुम coefficient a से divide करते हो — और अगर a negative है, तो symbol reverse करना ज़रूरी है। यहीं careful students careless से अलग होते हैं।
Step six — solution set को interval notation में लिखो।
और step seven — इसे number line पर दिखाओ, strict less-than या greater-than के लिए hollow circles, और or-equal versions के लिए filled circles चुनकर।

title: Proof: why dividing by a negative reverses the sign

board_content.text: Why the flip is not just a convention
Start from the meaning of order: $a < b$ means precisely that $b - a$ is a positive number.
Take any negative $c < 0$. A positive number times a negative number is negative:
Distribute: $cb - ca < 0$, so $cb < ca$, which is the same as $ca > cb$.
We started with $a<b$ and ended with $ca>cb$. The direction genuinely flipped. ∎

segments_english.text: You have been told to flip on a negative. Let me prove it, so it stops feeling like a rule you memorise and starts feeling like something you understand.
Everything rests on what less-than actually means. Saying a is less than b is precisely saying that b minus a is a positive number.
There it is on the board: a less than b if and only if b minus a is greater than zero.
Now take any negative number c. A positive number multiplied by a negative number is negative — that is basic sign arithmetic.
So c times the quantity b minus a is less than zero.
Distribute the c: c b minus c a is less than zero. Move c a across, and c b is less than c a — which is exactly the same as c a is greater than c b.
Look at where we are. We began with a less than b, and we ended with c a greater than c b.
The direction genuinely reversed. This is not a trick and not a convention to be memorised — it follows directly from what less-than means. And that is your proof.

segments_hinglish.text: तुम्हें बताया गया है कि negative पर flip करो। मैं इसे prove करता हूँ, ताकि ये rote rule की तरह ना लगे और तुम्हें समझ में आए।
सब कुछ इस पर टिका है कि less-than का असल में मतलब क्या है। a is less than b कहना का ठीक मतलब है कि b minus a एक positive number है।
बोर्ड पर यही है — a less than b, if and only if, b minus a greater than zero।
अब कोई भी negative number c लो। एक positive number को negative number से multiply करने पर negative आता है — ये basic sign arithmetic है।
तो c times the quantity b minus a, less than zero है।
c को distribute करो — c b minus c a less than zero। c a को दूसरी तरफ़ ले जाओ, तो c b less than c a — जो बिलकुल वही है जो c a greater than c b।
देखो हम कहाँ पहुँचे। हमने शुरू किया a less than b से, और ख़त्म किया c a greater than c b पर।
Direction सचमुच उल्टी हो गई। ये कोई trick नहीं, कोई rote convention नहीं — ये सीधे उसी से निकलता है कि less-than का मतलब क्या है। और यही तुम्हारा proof है।

title: Compound inequalities: move all three parts together

board_content.text: A double inequality is a single object
Treat all three parts as one chain: whatever you do to the middle, do identically to BOTH ends.
If a step multiplies by a negative, the WHOLE chain reverses and the two endpoints swap roles.
Then re-read the reversed chain left-to-right to state the answer cleanly.
The classic error: operating on only the middle and one end, leaving the third part behind.

segments_english.text: Sometimes the variable is trapped in the middle, like p is less-than-or-equal to some expression, which is less-than-or-equal to q. This is a compound, or double, inequality.
There it sits on the board — three parts at once.
The golden rule is to treat it as a single object with three parts. Whatever operation you apply to the middle, you apply identically to both ends. Never touch just one side.
And here is the subtle bit. If a step requires multiplying or dividing by a negative, the entire chain reverses — and crucially, the two endpoints swap their roles.
So p less-than-or-equal, dot dot dot, less-than-or-equal q becomes greater-than-or-equal, dot dot dot, greater-than-or-equal, running the other way.
You then simply re-read that reversed chain from left to right, and write the answer in its natural order.
The single most common error here is operating on only the middle and one end, and forgetting the third part. Keep all three moving in lockstep.

segments_hinglish.text: कभी-कभी variable बीच में फँसा होता है, जैसे p less-than-or-equal किसी expression से, जो less-than-or-equal q से। ये एक compound, या double, inequality है।
बोर्ड पर यही बैठी है — तीनों parts एक साथ।
Golden rule ये है कि इसे तीन parts वाला एक single object मानो। जो operation middle पर लगाओ, वही बिलकुल दोनों ends पर लगाओ। सिर्फ़ एक side को कभी मत छुओ।
और यहाँ subtle बात है। अगर किसी step में negative से multiply या divide करना पड़े, तो पूरी chain reverse हो जाती है — और सबसे ज़रूरी, दोनों endpoints अपने roles swap कर लेते हैं।
तो p less-than-or-equal, dot dot dot, less-than-or-equal q बन जाता है greater-than-or-equal, dot dot dot, greater-than-or-equal, उल्टी तरफ़ चलता हुआ।
फिर तुम बस उस reversed chain को left to right दोबारा पढ़ो, और answer को उसके natural order में लिखो।
यहाँ सबसे common error यही है — सिर्फ़ middle और एक end पर operate करना, और तीसरा part भूल जाना। तीनों को साथ-साथ चलाओ।

title: The order axioms and the language of intervals

board_content.text: The order axioms — your rulebook

board_content.latex: a < b \;\Rightarrow\; a + c < b + c
a < b,\; c > 0 \;\Rightarrow\; ac < bc \;\text{ and }\; \tfrac{a}{c} < \tfrac{b}{c}
a < b,\; c < 0 \;\Rightarrow\; ac > bc \;\text{ and }\; \tfrac{a}{c} > \tfrac{b}{c}
a < b \;\text{ and }\; b < c \;\Rightarrow\; a < c

board_content.text: General linear inequality

board_content.latex: ax + b > 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \begin{cases} x > -\tfrac{b}{a}, & a > 0 \\[4pt] x < -\tfrac{b}{a}, & a < 0 \end{cases}

board_content.text: Three equivalent languages: number line, set-builder $\{x : x \ge a\}$, and interval $[a, \infty)$.
Square bracket [ ] includes; round ( ) excludes. $\infty$ always gets a round bracket.

segments_english.text: These order axioms are the closest thing this subtopic has to formulas, so let me read each one out loud.
First: if a is less than b, then a plus c is less than b plus c. In words, adding the same c to both sides changes nothing.
Second: if a is less than b and c is positive, then a times c is less than b times c, and dividing keeps the direction too. Positive scaling preserves order.
Third, and this is the one that costs marks: if a is less than b but c is negative, then a times c is greater than b times c. The sign reverses.
Fourth is transitivity: if a is less than b, and b is less than c, then a is less than c. Order chains through.
From these follows the general linear inequality.
For a x plus b greater than zero: if a is positive, x is greater than negative b over a; if a is negative, x is less than negative b over a — the flip again, built right in.
And every answer should be sayable in three equivalent languages: as a shaded number line, in set-builder form as the set of x such that x is at least a, and as an interval, a to infinity.

One rigor checkpoint you must never miss: a square bracket includes the endpoint, a round bracket excludes it, and infinity always takes a round bracket. Writing three-to-infinity with a square bracket is always wrong.

segments_hinglish.text: ये order axioms इस subtopic के सबसे क़रीबी formulas हैं, तो मैं हर एक को ज़ोर से पढ़ता हूँ।
पहला — अगर a less than b है, तो a plus c less than b plus c है। यानी, दोनों sides में same c add करने से कुछ नहीं बदलता।
दूसरा — अगर a less than b है और c positive है, तो a times c less than b times c, और divide करने पर भी direction वही रहती है। Positive scaling order को बचाए रखता है।
तीसरा, और यही marks खाता है — अगर a less than b है पर c negative है, तो a times c greater than b times c हो जाता है। Sign उल्टा।
चौथा है transitivity — अगर a less than b, और b less than c, तो a less than c। Order chain हो जाता है।
इन्हीं से general linear inequality निकलती है।
a x plus b greater than zero के लिए — अगर a positive है, x greater than negative b over a; अगर a negative है, x less than negative b over a — वही flip, formula में ही अंदर।
और हर answer तीन equivalent languages में कहा जाना चाहिए — shaded number line, set-builder में यानी वो सारे x जिनके लिए x कम से कम a हो, और interval में, a to infinity।

एक rigor checkpoint कभी मत भूलना — square bracket endpoint को include करता है, round bracket उसे exclude करता है, और infinity हमेशा round bracket लेता है। Three-to-infinity को square bracket से लिखना हमेशा ग़लत है।

title: Worked example: solve and represent (CBSE)

board_content.text: Solve $3(2x-1) \ge 2(x+3) - 5$ and show it on a number line
Remove the brackets on both sides by distributing.
Collect terms: add 3, subtract $2x$ — both are safe moves.
Divide by $+4$ — a positive number, so no flip.

segments_english.text: Let us run the algorithm on a genuine C B S E board question. Solve three times the quantity two x minus one, greater-than-or-equal to two times the quantity x plus three, minus five, and then represent the answer on a number line.
First, remove the brackets by distributing on both sides.
On the left, six x minus three. On the right, two x plus six minus five, which tidies to two x plus one. So six x minus three is greater-than-or-equal to two x plus one.
Now collect the terms. Add three to both sides and subtract two x from both sides — both are addition-type moves, so both are completely safe.
That leaves four x greater-than-or-equal to four.
Divide both sides by positive four. Since four is positive, there is no flip to worry about.
And we land on x greater-than-or-equal to one, which in interval notation is one to infinity, with a square bracket on the one because it is included.
On the number line, that is a filled circle at one — filled, because one satisfies the or-equal — and the shading runs to the right, all the way to positive infinity.

segments_hinglish.text: चलो algorithm को एक असली C B S E board question पर चलाते हैं। Solve करो three times the quantity two x minus one, greater-than-or-equal to two times the quantity x plus three, minus five, और फिर answer को number line पर दिखाओ।
पहले, दोनों sides पर distribute करके brackets हटाओ।
Left पर six x minus three। Right पर two x plus six minus five, जो साफ़ होकर two x plus one बनता है। तो six x minus three greater-than-or-equal to two x plus one।
अब terms collect करो। दोनों sides में three add करो और two x subtract करो — दोनों addition-type moves हैं, तो दोनों बिलकुल safe।
इससे बचता है four x greater-than-or-equal to four।
दोनों sides को positive four से divide करो। चूँकि four positive है, यहाँ flip की कोई चिंता नहीं।
और हम पहुँचते हैं x greater-than-or-equal to one पर, जो interval notation में one to infinity है, one पर square bracket के साथ क्योंकि वो included है।
Number line पर, ये one पर एक filled circle है — filled, क्योंकि one or-equal को satisfy करता है — और shading right की तरफ़ चलती है, बिलकुल positive infinity तक।

title: Worked example: the divide-by-negative speed trap

board_content.text: Solve $-7 \le \dfrac{3-2x}{4} < 5$
Two traps at once: a compound inequality AND a divide-by-negative.
Multiply all three parts by 4 (positive — directions hold).
Subtract 3 from all three parts.
Divide all three by $-2$ — flip both symbols, and the whole chain reverses.
The strict end landed low, the filled end high — exactly what the endpoint swap predicts.

segments_english.text: This one is a J E E Main speed trap, and it fires two hazards at once. Solve negative seven less-than-or-equal to the quantity three minus two x, over four, which is strictly less than five.
Both traps are live: it is a compound inequality, and it will force a divide-by-negative. Move fast, but flip carefully.
First, multiply all three parts by four. Four is positive, so every direction holds.
That gives negative twenty eight less-than-or-equal to three minus two x, less than twenty.
Next, subtract three from all three parts.
Now we have negative thirty one less-than-or-equal to negative two x, less than seventeen.
The dangerous step: divide all three parts by negative two. Both symbols flip, and the whole chain reverses.

Reading the reversed chain back left-to-right gives negative seventeen-halves, strictly less than x, less-than-or-equal to thirty one-halves. So the answer is the interval from negative seventeen-halves, open, to thirty one-halves, closed.

<excited>And here is the beautiful check.</excited> The strict less-than rode in on the five side and ended up on the lower bound; the or-equal rode in on the negative seven side and ended up on the upper bound. If your brackets came out the other way, you forgot to swap inclusivity along with the symbols.

segments_hinglish.text: ये एक J E E Main speed trap है, और ये एक साथ दो hazards चलाता है। Solve करो negative seven less-than-or-equal to the quantity three minus two x, over four, जो strictly less than five है।
दोनों traps live हैं — ये compound inequality है, और ये divide-by-negative कराएगा। Fast चलो, पर flip carefully।
पहले, तीनों parts को four से multiply करो। Four positive है, तो हर direction वही रहती है।
इससे मिलता है negative twenty eight less-than-or-equal to three minus two x, less than twenty।
अब, तीनों parts में से three subtract करो।
अब हमारे पास है negative thirty one less-than-or-equal to negative two x, less than seventeen।
Dangerous step — तीनों parts को negative two से divide करो। दोनों symbols flip, और पूरी chain reverse।

उस reversed chain को वापस left-to-right पढ़ने पर मिलता है negative seventeen-halves, strictly less than x, less-than-or-equal to thirty one-halves। तो answer है interval negative seventeen-halves, open, से thirty one-halves, closed तक।

<excited>और ये रहा शानदार check।</excited> Strict less-than five वाली side से आया और lower bound पर पहुँचा; or-equal negative seven वाली side से आया और upper bound पर पहुँचा। अगर तुम्हारे brackets उल्टे आए, तो तुम symbols के साथ inclusivity swap करना भूल गए।

title: Worked example: intersect two solutions, then count integers

board_content.text: Integers satisfying both $3x-2>4$ and $2(x-1)\le x+3$
The system needs BOTH true, so intersect the two solution sets.
Now translate a continuous interval into a discrete integer count.
2 is excluded (strict); 5 is included (non-strict). Integers: 3, 4, 5.

segments_english.text: Here is a multi-concept J E E Main problem: find how many integer values of x satisfy both inequalities at once, and then find their sum. Solving each one is routine — the marks live in what you do afterwards.
First inequality: three x minus two is greater than four. Add two, and three x is greater than six, so x is greater than two.
Second inequality: expand two times x minus one to get two x minus two, less-than-or-equal to x plus three. Subtract x, add two, and you get x less-than-or-equal to five.
Now, the word both matters enormously. The system demands that both hold, so we intersect the two solution sets, not combine them.
x greater than two, and x less-than-or-equal to five, gives the interval from two, open, to five, closed.
And here comes the real move — translating that continuous interval into a discrete count of integers.
Watch the endpoints. Two is excluded because the first inequality was strict; five is included because the second was non-strict. So the integers inside are three, four, and five.
That is a count of three, and their sum is three plus four plus five, which is twelve.

segments_hinglish.text: ये एक multi-concept J E E Main problem है — निकालो कि x की कितनी integer values दोनों inequalities को एक साथ satisfy करती हैं, और फिर उनका sum। हर एक को solve करना routine है — marks उसके बाद वाले काम में हैं।
पहली inequality — three x minus two greater than four। Two add करो, तो three x greater than six, यानी x greater than two।
दूसरी inequality — two times x minus one को expand करो, मिलता है two x minus two, less-than-or-equal to x plus three। x subtract करो, two add करो, तो x less-than-or-equal to five।
अब, both शब्द बहुत मायने रखता है। System माँगता है कि दोनों hold करें, तो हम दोनों solution sets को intersect करते हैं, combine नहीं।
x greater than two, और x less-than-or-equal to five, देता है interval two, open, से five, closed तक।
और यहाँ असली move आता है — उस continuous interval को integers की discrete count में translate करना।
Endpoints देखो। Two excluded है क्योंकि पहली inequality strict थी; five included है क्योंकि दूसरी non-strict थी। तो अंदर के integers हैं three, four, और five।
तो count है three, और उनका sum है three plus four plus five, यानी twelve।

title: Worked example: the parameter that makes it true for every x (JEE Advanced)

board_content.text: Find all $a$: $a(x-1) < 2x+3$ holds for every real $x$
Expand and gather the $x$-terms on one side.
Everything hinges on the coefficient $(a-2)$ — and the deep step is realising it can vanish.
$a = 2$: the inequality collapses to $0 \cdot x < 5$, i.e. $0 < 5$ — true for EVERY x.
Insight: a 'linear' inequality stops being linear the instant its leading coefficient is zero.

segments_english.text: Now a J E E Advanced problem, and it hides a genuinely clever idea. Find all real values of the parameter a for which a times the quantity x minus one is less than two x plus three, holds for every single real number x.
Start by expanding, and gather the x-terms onto one side.
You get a x minus a is less than two x plus three, and rearranging, the quantity a minus two, times x, is less than a plus three.
Everything now hinges on the coefficient of x, which is a minus two — and the deep step is realising that this coefficient can actually vanish. So we split into three cases.
If a minus two is positive, meaning a is greater than two, dividing gives x less than some fixed number. That is only a half-line, not all of the real line. Rejected.
If a minus two is negative, meaning a is less than two, dividing flips the sign to x greater than that number — again just a half-line. Rejected.

But if a minus two equals zero, meaning a equals two, the inequality collapses. The x-term disappears entirely, and you are left with zero is less than five — which is true for every x, no matter what x is.
So the answer is a single value: a equals two.

<curious>And why is this Advanced-level?</curious> Because the key insight is that a linear inequality stops being linear the instant its leading coefficient hits zero, and that degenerate case — usually just a nuisance — is the only one that gives the universal solution we wanted.

segments_hinglish.text: अब एक J E E Advanced problem, और इसमें एक सचमुच clever idea छिपा है। Parameter a की सारी real values निकालो जिनके लिए a times the quantity x minus one, less than two x plus three, हर एक real number x के लिए hold करे।
Expand करके शुरू करो, और x-terms को एक side पर इकट्ठा करो।
मिलता है a x minus a less than two x plus three, और rearrange करने पर, the quantity a minus two, times x, less than a plus three।
अब सब कुछ x के coefficient पर टिका है, जो है a minus two — और deep step ये समझना है कि ये coefficient सचमुच vanish हो सकता है। तो तीन cases में बाँटते हैं।
अगर a minus two positive है, यानी a greater than two, तो divide करने पर x less than एक fixed number। ये सिर्फ़ एक half-line है, पूरी real line नहीं। Rejected।
अगर a minus two negative है, यानी a less than two, तो divide करने पर sign flip होकर x greater than वो number — फिर सिर्फ़ half-line। Rejected।
पर अगर a minus two equals zero, यानी a equals two, तो inequality collapse हो जाती है। x-term पूरी तरह ग़ायब, और बचता है zero less than five — जो हर x के लिए true है, चाहे x कुछ भी हो।
तो answer एक ही value है — a equals two।

<curious>और ये Advanced-level क्यों है?</curious> क्योंकि key insight ये है कि linear inequality उसी पल linear रहना छोड़ देती है जब उसका leading coefficient zero हो जाता है, और वो degenerate case — आमतौर पर बस एक nuisance — ही एकमात्र है जो वो universal solution देता है जो हमें चाहिए था।

title: Pitfalls and the 10-second sanity check

board_content.text: Where the marks leak away
Forgetting to flip on a negative — by far the costliest mistake.
Build the reflex: see a negative coefficient → flip before you write the next line.
Cross-multiplying by a variable like $x+3$ is illegal — its sign is unknown. Bring everything to one side.
< > are always hollow/round; $\le$ $\ge$ always filled/square; $\infty$ is always round.
In a double inequality, operate on all three parts — never leave one end behind.
Pro-tip: pick any number inside your interval and substitute back into the original.

segments_english.text: Let me close this subtopic with the mistakes that quietly cost the most marks, and one habit that catches almost all of them.
By far the costliest error is forgetting to flip the sign when you multiply or divide by a negative. This single slip turns a correct method into a wrong answer.
So build a reflex. The moment you see a negative coefficient about to divide, flip the symbol before you write the next line. Make it automatic.

The second trap: cross-multiplying by a variable expression like x plus three. Its sign is unknown, so you cannot tell whether to flip. Always bring everything to one side and combine into a single fraction instead.
The third: mixing up circles and brackets. Less-than and greater-than are always hollow and round; the or-equal versions are always filled and square; and infinity always takes a round bracket.
The fourth: breaking a double inequality apart. Operate on all three parts together, and never leave one end behind.
<whisper>And here is the ten-second habit that saves you.</whisper> After you find an interval, pick any number inside it and substitute it back into the original inequality.

Take our earlier answer, the interval from negative seventeen-halves to thirty one-halves. Test x equals zero: the expression becomes three-quarters, which is nought point seven five, and indeed negative seven is at most nought point seven five, which is below five. It checks out — your direction and brackets are almost certainly right.

segments_hinglish.text: इस subtopic को उन mistakes के साथ ख़त्म करते हैं जो चुपचाप सबसे ज़्यादा marks खाती हैं, और एक habit जो लगभग सबको पकड़ लेती है।
अब तक की सबसे costly error है — negative से multiply या divide करते वक़्त sign flip करना भूल जाना। ये एक slip सही method को ग़लत answer में बदल देती है।
तो एक reflex बनाओ। जिस पल negative coefficient divide करने वाला दिखे, अगली line लिखने से पहले symbol flip करो। इसे automatic बना दो।

दूसरा trap — किसी variable expression, जैसे x plus three, से cross-multiply करना। उसका sign पता नहीं, तो flip करना है या नहीं ये तय नहीं कर सकते। हमेशा सब कुछ एक side लाकर single fraction में combine करो।
तीसरा — circles और brackets को mix करना। Less-than और greater-than हमेशा hollow और round; or-equal versions हमेशा filled और square; और infinity हमेशा round bracket लेता है।
चौथा — double inequality को तोड़ना। तीनों parts पर साथ operate करो, और कोई end कभी पीछे मत छोड़ो।
<whisper>और ये रही वो ten-second habit जो तुम्हें बचाती है।</whisper> Interval मिलने के बाद, उसके अंदर कोई भी number लो और उसे original inequality में वापस substitute करो।

हमारा पहला answer लो, interval negative seventeen-halves से thirty one-halves तक। Test करो x equals zero — expression बनता है three-quarters, यानी zero point seven five, और सचमुच negative seven at most zero point seven five है, जो five से नीचे है। सही निकला — तुम्हारी direction और brackets लगभग पक्के सही हैं।

title: The answer gains a dimension: half-planes

board_content.text: One variable → two variables
In one variable, a linear inequality carved out a stretch of the number line.
Add a second variable and the solution becomes an entire flat region of the plane.
This single line slices the whole plane into two pieces — each is a half-plane.
Every point sits in exactly one place: on the line, or in one of the two half-planes.
A two-variable inequality answers with a REGION, never a point.

segments_english.text: In the last subtopic, a linear inequality in one variable carved out a stretch of the one-dimensional number line. Now we add a second variable, and something rather beautiful happens.
Recall that in one variable, the answer was always an interval — a segment of a single line.
Add a second variable, and the answer grows a dimension. It is no longer a stretch of a line; it becomes an entire flat region of the two-dimensional plane.
Here is the picture to hold in your head. Draw the line x plus y equals four on graph paper.
That single line slices the whole plane cleanly into two pieces, like a knife through a roti. Each piece is called a half-plane.
Now every point in the plane sits in exactly one of three places — on the line itself, in the half-plane on one side, or in the half-plane on the other side.
So a linear inequality like x plus y less than four is simply asking: give me all the points on one particular side.
And that is the whole shift — a two-variable inequality always answers with a region, never with a single point.

segments_hinglish.text: पिछले subtopic में, एक variable की linear inequality one-dimensional number line का एक हिस्सा काटती थी। अब हम एक दूसरा variable जोड़ते हैं, और कुछ बहुत ख़ूबसूरत होता है।
याद करो — एक variable में answer हमेशा एक interval था, एक single line का एक segment।
एक दूसरा variable जोड़ो, और answer एक dimension बढ़ा लेता है। अब वो line का हिस्सा नहीं, बल्कि two-dimensional plane का एक पूरा flat region बन जाता है।
ये रहा वो picture जो दिमाग़ में रखना है। Graph paper पर line x plus y equals four बनाओ।
वो एक line पूरे plane को साफ़ दो टुकड़ों में काट देती है, जैसे रोटी पर चाकू। हर टुकड़ा कहलाता है half-plane।
अब plane का हर point ठीक तीन में से एक जगह पर है — या line पर, या एक side के half-plane में, या दूसरी side के half-plane में।
तो x plus y less than four जैसी inequality बस ये पूछ रही है — मुझे एक ख़ास side के सारे points दो।
और यही पूरा shift है — two-variable inequality का answer हमेशा एक region होता है, कभी single point नहीं।

title: Why one test point decides an entire side

board_content.text: The budget region, and the one-point trick
A register costs ₹40, a pen ₹20, and you have ₹120 to spend.
3 registers (₹120), 2 registers + 1 pen (₹100), or nothing — all valid $(x,y)$ pairs.
Plot them all and they fill a whole triangular patch — the solution region.
A linear expression keeps the SAME sign throughout each side of the line.
So test ONE point (usually the origin) — it reports for the entire half-plane.

segments_english.text: Let me make this concrete with a shopping trip. Suppose you have one hundred twenty rupees to spend at a stationery shop, where a register costs forty rupees and a pen costs twenty rupees.
If you buy x registers and y pens, your spending is forty x plus twenty y, and staying within budget means forty x plus twenty y is at most one hundred twenty.
Notice this on the board — it is an inequality, not an equation, because you can spend less than the limit.
There is no single answer. Three registers and no pens costs exactly one hundred twenty. Two registers and one pen costs one hundred, comfortably under. Or you buy nothing at all.
Every one of these is a valid x-y pair, and if you plotted all of them, they would fill a whole triangular patch of the plane. That patch is the solution region.

Now here is the genius of the method. Because a straight line divides the plane into just two sides, and a linear expression keeps the same sign right across each side, you never have to test infinitely many points.
You only need to test one convenient point — usually the origin, since zero-zero is easiest. Substitute it, and one answer decides the fate of an entire half-plane.
On the board I have drawn the region: the line, and the triangular patch below it that stays within your budget.

segments_hinglish.text: इसे एक shopping trip से concrete बनाते हैं। मान लो तुम्हारे पास stationery shop में खर्च करने के लिए one hundred twenty rupees हैं, जहाँ register forty rupees का है और pen twenty rupees का।
अगर तुम x registers और y pens ख़रीदो, तो तुम्हारा खर्च है forty x plus twenty y, और budget के अंदर रहने का मतलब है forty x plus twenty y at most one hundred twenty।
बोर्ड पर देखो — ये inequality है, equation नहीं, क्योंकि तुम limit से कम भी खर्च कर सकते हो।
यहाँ कोई single answer नहीं है। Three registers और कोई pen नहीं — बिलकुल one hundred twenty। Two registers और one pen — one hundred, आराम से under। या कुछ भी मत ख़रीदो।
इनमें से हर एक valid x-y pair है, और अगर तुम सबको plot करो, तो वो plane का एक पूरा triangular patch भर देंगे। वही patch है solution region।

अब यहाँ है method की असली ख़ूबी। चूँकि एक straight line plane को सिर्फ़ दो sides में बाँटती है, और linear expression हर side पर same sign रखता है, तुम्हें कभी infinitely many points test नहीं करने पड़ते।
तुम्हें सिर्फ़ एक convenient point test करना है — आमतौर पर origin, क्योंकि zero-zero सबसे आसान है। उसे substitute करो, और एक answer पूरे half-plane का फ़ैसला कर देता है।
बोर्ड पर मैंने region बना दिया है — line, और उसके नीचे वो triangular patch जो तुम्हारे budget के अंदर रहता है।

title: The four working rules

board_content.text: Boundary, line style, test point, system
Boundary line: replace the inequality sign with = and draw $ax+by=c$.
Line style: $\le$ or $\ge$ → solid (boundary included); < or > → dotted (excluded).
Test-point rule: pick a point off the line. Satisfies → shade its side; fails → shade the other.
System of inequalities → shade the intersection: the area satisfying every one at once.
Real problems add $x \ge 0,\ y \ge 0$, confining the region to the first quadrant.
(0,0) fails when the line passes through the origin — then pick (1,0) or (0,1).

segments_english.text: Let us pin down the four rules that run this entire subtopic. Learn these and every graphical question becomes mechanical.
Rule one, the boundary line. Replace the inequality sign with an equals sign and draw the line a x plus b y equals c. That line is the border between the two sides.

Rule two, line style, and this carries presentation marks. If the inequality is less-than-or-equal or greater-than-or-equal, the boundary is included, so draw it solid. If it is strictly less-than or greater-than, the boundary is excluded, so draw it dotted.
Rule three, the test-point rule. Choose any point not on the line. If it satisfies the inequality, shade the half-plane containing it. If it fails, shade the other half-plane.
Rule four, systems. When you have several inequalities at once, the solution is the intersection — the overlap — the region satisfying every inequality simultaneously, not the combined shading.

And in real-world problems, quantities like units produced or articles bought cannot be negative, so you add x greater-than-or-equal to zero and y greater-than-or-equal to zero, which confines everything to the first quadrant.

<curious>One warning worth burning into memory.</curious> The origin is your favourite test point, but it fails completely when the boundary line passes through the origin — then zero-zero sits on the line and cannot tell the two sides apart. In that case, pick one-zero or zero-one instead.

segments_hinglish.text: चलो उन चार rules को पक्का कर लें जो इस पूरे subtopic को चलाते हैं। इन्हें सीख लो और हर graphical question mechanical बन जाता है।
Rule one, boundary line। Inequality sign को equals sign से बदलो और line a x plus b y equals c बनाओ। वही line दोनों sides के बीच की border है।

Rule two, line style, और ये presentation marks देता है। अगर inequality less-than-or-equal या greater-than-or-equal है, तो boundary included है, इसलिए solid बनाओ। अगर strictly less-than या greater-than है, तो boundary excluded है, इसलिए dotted बनाओ।
Rule three, test-point rule। कोई भी point चुनो जो line पर ना हो। अगर वो inequality satisfy करे, तो उसे रखने वाला half-plane shade करो। अगर fail करे, तो दूसरा half-plane।
Rule four, systems। जब कई inequalities एक साथ हों, तो solution है intersection — यानी overlap — वो region जो हर inequality को एक साथ satisfy करे, combined shading नहीं।

और real-world problems में, units produced या articles bought जैसी quantities negative नहीं हो सकतीं, इसलिए तुम x greater-than-or-equal to zero और y greater-than-or-equal to zero जोड़ते हो, जो सब कुछ first quadrant में समेट देता है।

<curious>एक warning जो दिमाग़ में गाड़ लो।</curious> Origin तुम्हारा favourite test point है, पर ये तब पूरी तरह fail हो जाता है जब boundary line origin से गुज़रती है — तब zero-zero line पर बैठा होता है और दोनों sides में फ़र्क़ नहीं बता सकता। ऐसे में one-zero या zero-one चुनो।

title: Bounded, unbounded, empty — and corner points

board_content.text: The shape of a solution region
A region may be bounded (finite area, like a triangle) or unbounded (extends forever).
A system can have an EMPTY solution set when the half-planes share no common point.
Corner points (vertices) are found by solving the boundary lines two at a time.
These vertices become decisive in Class 12 Linear Programming.
Solid line ⇔ filled circle; dotted line ⇔ hollow circle — one idea in two costumes.
So the strictness convention from the number line reappears here as line style.

segments_english.text: Before we solve examples, let us name the shapes a solution region can take — the vocabulary the exam expects.
A region can be bounded, meaning it is enclosed on all sides and has a finite area, like a triangle. Or it can be unbounded, extending infinitely in some direction.
A system can even have an empty solution set. That happens when the half-planes share no common point at all — the constraints contradict each other.
The corner points, or vertices, of a bounded region are found by solving the boundary lines two at a time — pairwise intersections.
These vertices are not just decoration. They become absolutely decisive next year, in Class twelve Linear Programming, where the best answer always sits at a corner.
And notice a lovely echo. A solid line corresponds to a filled circle, and a dotted line to a hollow circle. It is one single idea wearing two costumes.

So the very strictness convention you learned on the one-dimensional number line reappears here, in two dimensions, dressed up as line style. Nothing new to memorise — just recognised in a new setting.

segments_hinglish.text: Examples solve करने से पहले, चलो उन shapes को नाम दें जो एक solution region ले सकता है — वो vocabulary जो exam expect करता है।
एक region bounded हो सकता है, यानी हर तरफ़ से enclosed और finite area वाला, जैसे triangle। या unbounded हो सकता है, किसी direction में infinitely फैलता हुआ।
एक system का empty solution set भी हो सकता है। ये तब होता है जब half-planes का कोई common point ही ना हो — constraints एक-दूसरे को contradict करें।
एक bounded region के corner points, यानी vertices, boundary lines को दो-दो करके solve करके निकलते हैं — pairwise intersections।
ये vertices सिर्फ़ decoration नहीं हैं। अगले साल, Class twelve Linear Programming में, ये बिलकुल decisive बन जाते हैं, जहाँ best answer हमेशा किसी corner पर बैठता है।
और एक प्यारा echo देखो। Solid line का मतलब filled circle, और dotted line का मतलब hollow circle। ये एक ही idea है, दो costumes में।
तो वही strictness convention जो तुमने one-dimensional number line पर सीखा था, यहाँ two dimensions में line style बनकर लौट आता है। कुछ नया याद नहीं करना — बस नए रूप में पहचानना।

title: CBSE derivation: why the solution is a whole half-plane

board_content.text: Why an inequality corresponds to a half-plane
Claim: every point satisfying $ax+by>c$ (take $b>0$) lies in one half-plane of $ax+by=c$.
Take $P(\alpha,\beta)$ on the line, so $a\alpha + b\beta = c$.
Take $Q(\alpha,\gamma)$ directly above P, so $\gamma > \beta$. Since $b>0$: $b\gamma > b\beta$.
So Q satisfies $ax+by>c$. Every point above the line works — the forward direction.
The converse runs the steps backward: any solution point must lie above the line.
Sign of $ax+by-c$ is constant on each side — exactly why one test point suffices. ∎

segments_english.text: The test-and-shade recipe works, but a C B S E long-answer question may ask why a linear inequality corresponds to an entire half-plane. Here is the rigorous reason.
The claim: every point satisfying a x plus b y greater than c — and take b positive for definiteness — lies entirely in one of the two half-planes of the line a x plus b y equals c.
Set it up. Pick any point P, with coordinates alpha and beta, that lies on the line. Then a alpha plus b beta equals c exactly.

Now take a point Q directly above P — same x-coordinate alpha, but higher up, so gamma is greater than beta. Because b is positive, multiplying that inequality by b keeps its direction: b gamma is greater than b beta.
Add a alpha to both sides. The left becomes a alpha plus b gamma; the right is a alpha plus b beta, which by our setup is exactly c.

So a alpha plus b gamma is greater than c — meaning Q satisfies the inequality. And since Q was any point above the line, every point in the upper half-plane satisfies it. That is the forward direction.

The converse simply runs the same steps backward: if a point satisfies the inequality, the algebra forces it to lie above the line. Both directions together prove the solution is precisely one half-plane.

And the practical pay-off is huge. The sign of a x plus b y minus c is constant throughout each side, so one specimen point reports for its entire side. That is exactly why a single test point suffices.
The diagram makes it visual: P on the line, Q directly above it in the upper half-plane, labelled two.

segments_hinglish.text: Test-and-shade recipe काम करता है, पर एक C B S E long-answer question पूछ सकता है कि linear inequality एक पूरे half-plane से क्यों मेल खाती है। ये रही rigorous वजह।
Claim ये है — a x plus b y greater than c को satisfy करने वाला हर point, और definiteness के लिए b positive लो, line a x plus b y equals c के दो half-planes में से एक में ही होता है।
Setup करो। कोई भी point P लो, coordinates alpha और beta, जो line पर हो। तो a alpha plus b beta बिलकुल c के बराबर है।

अब P के ठीक ऊपर एक point Q लो — same x-coordinate alpha, पर ऊपर, तो gamma greater than beta। चूँकि b positive है, उस inequality को b से multiply करने पर direction वही रहती है — b gamma greater than b beta।
दोनों sides में a alpha add करो। Left बनता है a alpha plus b gamma; right है a alpha plus b beta, जो हमारे setup से बिलकुल c है।
तो a alpha plus b gamma greater than c — यानी Q inequality satisfy करता है। और चूँकि Q line के ऊपर कोई भी point था, upper half-plane का हर point इसे satisfy करता है। यही forward direction है।

Converse बस वही steps उल्टे चलाता है — अगर कोई point inequality satisfy करे, तो algebra उसे line के ऊपर होने पर मजबूर कर देता है। दोनों directions मिलकर prove करती हैं कि solution ठीक एक half-plane है।

और practical pay-off बहुत बड़ा है। a x plus b y minus c का sign हर side पर constant रहता है, तो एक specimen point अपनी पूरी side के लिए report कर देता है। यही असल वजह है कि single test point काफ़ी है।
Diagram इसे visual बना देता है — P line पर, Q उसके ठीक ऊपर upper half-plane में, जिस पर two लिखा है।

title: The key forms: general inequality, intercepts, shoelace

board_content.text: Forms to keep on hand
Draw the boundary $ax+by=c$ by plotting its two intercepts.
For the area of a bounded polygon, list vertices in cyclic order and use the shoelace formula.
List vertices in cyclic order before shoelace — a mis-ordered vertex ruins the area.

segments_english.text: This subtopic is graphical rather than formula-heavy, but a few forms are worth keeping on hand as a toolkit.

First, the general shape. A linear inequality in two variables is a x plus b y, then one of the four signs, then c — where a and b are not both zero. That last condition is what keeps it genuinely two-variable.
To draw the boundary, plot the line a x plus b y equals c using its two intercepts — the cleanest way to fix a straight line.
The intercepts are c-over-a comma zero on the x-axis, and zero comma c-over-b on the y-axis. Two points, one line.
And when a question asks for the area of a bounded region, list its vertices in cyclic order and apply the shoelace formula.

The shoelace formula: area equals one-half the absolute value of the sum, over all vertices, of x-i times y-i-plus-one minus x-i-plus-one times y-i. It sounds fearsome but it is just a bookkeeping sum around the corners.

<whisper>One caution that quietly ruins answers.</whisper> You must list the vertices in cyclic order — going around the polygon — before applying shoelace. A single vertex out of order throws off the entire area.

segments_hinglish.text: ये subtopic formula-heavy से ज़्यादा graphical है, पर कुछ forms toolkit की तरह हाथ में रखने लायक़ हैं।
पहला, general shape। Two variables की linear inequality है a x plus b y, फिर चार signs में से एक, फिर c — जहाँ a और b दोनों zero नहीं हैं। वही आख़िरी condition इसे सचमुच two-variable रखती है।
Boundary बनाने के लिए, line a x plus b y equals c को उसके दो intercepts से plot करो — straight line को fix करने का सबसे साफ़ तरीक़ा।
Intercepts हैं c-over-a comma zero, x-axis पर, और zero comma c-over-b, y-axis पर। दो points, एक line।
और जब कोई question bounded region का area माँगे, तो उसके vertices को cyclic order में लिखो और shoelace formula लगाओ।

Shoelace formula — area equals one-half the absolute value of the sum, सारे vertices पर, x-i times y-i-plus-one minus x-i-plus-one times y-i का। सुनने में डरावना है, पर ये बस corners के around एक bookkeeping sum है।

<whisper>एक caution जो चुपचाप answers बिगाड़ देता है।</whisper> Shoelace लगाने से पहले vertices को cyclic order में लिखना ज़रूरी है — polygon के around घूमते हुए। एक भी vertex order से बाहर, तो पूरा area ग़लत।

title: Worked example: solve 2x+3y ≤ 12 graphically (CBSE)

board_content.text: Solve $2x + 3y \le 12$ graphically
Boundary $2x+3y=12$. Intercepts: $y=0 \Rightarrow x=6$; $x=0 \Rightarrow y=4$.
The sign is $\le$, so draw the line solid — the boundary is included.
The line misses the origin, so test $(0,0)$: $2(0)+3(0)=0$.
True — so shade the half-plane containing the origin (below-left of the line).
Solution: all points on or below $2x+3y=12$, boundary included.

segments_english.text: Let us run the full recipe on a standard C B S E question. Solve two x plus three y less-than-or-equal to twelve, graphically.

Start with the boundary line, two x plus three y equals twelve, and find its intercepts. Put y equals zero and you get x equals six, the point six comma zero. Put x equals zero and you get y equals four, the point zero comma four.
The inequality sign is less-than-or-equal, which includes equality, so the boundary belongs to the solution — draw the line solid.
The line does not pass through the origin, so the origin is a perfectly good test point. Substitute zero and zero: two times zero plus three times zero is zero.
So we are checking whether zero is at most twelve.
It is true — zero is comfortably less than twelve. So we shade the half-plane that contains the origin, the side below and to the left of the line.
And that is the answer: all points on or below the line two x plus three y equals twelve, with the boundary itself included.
The diagram shows it cleanly — the solid line through six comma zero and zero comma four, with the origin side shaded.

Boundary line से शुरू करो, two x plus three y equals twelve, और उसके intercepts निकालो। y equals zero रखो तो x equals six, यानी point six comma zero। x equals zero रखो तो y equals four, यानी point zero comma four।
Inequality sign less-than-or-equal है, जो equality include करता है, तो boundary solution का हिस्सा है — line solid बनाओ।
Line origin से नहीं गुज़रती, तो origin एक बढ़िया test point है। Zero और zero substitute करो — two times zero plus three times zero, यानी zero।
तो हम check कर रहे हैं कि zero at most twelve है या नहीं।
ये true है — zero आराम से twelve से कम है। तो हम वो half-plane shade करते हैं जिसमें origin है, line के नीचे और बाईं तरफ़ वाली side।
और यही answer है — line two x plus three y equals twelve पर या उसके नीचे के सारे points, boundary समेत।

title: Worked example: y > 2x, the origin-on-the-line trap

board_content.text: Solve $y > 2x$ graphically
Trap: the boundary $y=2x$ passes through the origin — so (0,0) is useless.
Substituting (0,0) gives $0 > 0$, false — but that decides neither side.
Pick another off-line point, say $(1,0)$: is $0 > 2(1)$? No.
So $(1,0)$ is NOT in the region — shade the other side.
Confirm with $(0,1)$: is $1 > 0$? Yes — and $(0,1)$ sits on that other side.
Sign is strict >, so draw the line dotted. Solution: the open half-plane above $y=2x$.

segments_english.text: This is a J E E Main speed trap, and it catches students on autopilot. Solve y greater than two x, graphically.
Here is the trap. Rewrite it as negative two x plus y greater than zero if you like — the point is that the boundary, y equals two x, passes straight through the origin.
So if you reach for zero-zero out of habit, substituting gives zero greater than zero, which is false — but that tells you nothing about either side, because the origin is sitting right on the line.
The fix is to pick any other point that is off the line. Say one comma zero. Ask: is zero greater than two times one? Is zero greater than two? No, it is not.
So the point one-zero is not in the region. That means we shade the other side, away from one-zero.
Let us confirm with the point zero comma one. Is one greater than zero? Yes. And zero-one does sit on that other side — so the shading is consistent.
Finally, the sign is a strict greater-than, so the boundary is excluded — draw the line dotted. The solution is the open half-plane lying above the line y equals two x.
The diagram captures it: the dotted line through the origin, the region above it shaded, one-zero marked as failing and zero-one as working.

segments_hinglish.text: ये एक J E E Main speed trap है, और ये autopilot पर चल रहे students को पकड़ लेता है। Solve करो y greater than two x, graphically।
यहाँ है trap। चाहो तो इसे negative two x plus y greater than zero लिख लो — बात ये है कि boundary, y equals two x, सीधे origin से गुज़रती है।
तो अगर आदतन zero-zero उठाओगे, substitute करने पर मिलता है zero greater than zero, जो false है — पर ये किसी side के बारे में कुछ नहीं बताता, क्योंकि origin तो line पर ही बैठा है।
Fix ये है कि कोई और point चुनो जो line पर ना हो। मान लो one comma zero। पूछो — क्या zero greater than two times one है? क्या zero greater than two है? नहीं।
तो point one-zero region में नहीं है। इसका मतलब हम दूसरी side shade करते हैं, one-zero से दूर वाली।
Point zero comma one से confirm करते हैं। क्या one greater than zero है? हाँ। और zero-one उसी दूसरी side पर बैठता है — तो shading consistent है।
आख़िर में, sign strict greater-than है, तो boundary excluded है — line dotted बनाओ। Solution है line y equals two x के ऊपर वाला open half-plane।
Diagram इसे पकड़ लेता है — origin से गुज़रती dotted line, उसके ऊपर का region shaded, one-zero fail होता हुआ और zero-one काम करता हुआ।

segments_english.text: Now a J E E Main problem that mixes inequalities with a little coordinate geometry. Find the corner points, the vertices, of the region defined by three constraints: x plus y at most four, x at least one, and y at least zero.
The key idea: each constraint is a half-plane, and the feasible region is their overlap — the area satisfying all three at once.

Let us read the three half-planes. x plus y at most four means on or below that slanting line. x at least one means on or to the right of the vertical line x equals one. And y at least zero means on or above the x-axis.

Their overlap is a bounded triangle, and its vertices are simply the pairwise intersections of the boundary lines. This is where the coordinate-geometry skill enters — you solve pairs of simultaneous equations.
First pair: the vertical line x equals one meets the x-axis y equals zero at the point one comma zero.
Second pair: the slant line x plus y equals four meets y equals zero at four comma zero. Third pair: x plus y equals four meets x equals one at one comma three.
So the three vertices are one-zero, four-zero, and one-three, and the region is a bounded triangle — a finite patch, not something that runs off to infinity.
The diagram shows all three boundary lines and the shaded triangle they enclose, with each corner labelled.

segments_hinglish.text: अब एक J E E Main problem जो inequalities को थोड़ी coordinate geometry के साथ mix करता है। निकालो उस region के corner points, यानी vertices, जो तीन constraints से बना है — x plus y at most four, x at least one, और y at least zero।
Key idea — हर constraint एक half-plane है, और feasible region उनका overlap है, वो area जो तीनों को एक साथ satisfy करे।

तीनों half-planes पढ़ते हैं। x plus y at most four का मतलब उस slanting line पर या उसके नीचे। x at least one का मतलब vertical line x equals one पर या उसके दाईं तरफ़। और y at least zero का मतलब x-axis पर या उसके ऊपर।
इनका overlap एक bounded triangle है, और उसके vertices बस boundary lines के pairwise intersections हैं। यहीं coordinate-geometry skill आती है — तुम simultaneous equations के pairs solve करते हो।
पहला pair — vertical line x equals one, x-axis y equals zero से मिलती है point one comma zero पर।
दूसरा pair — slant line x plus y equals four, y equals zero से मिलती है four comma zero पर। तीसरा pair — x plus y equals four, x equals one से मिलती है one comma three पर।
तो तीनों vertices हैं one-zero, four-zero, और one-three, और region एक bounded triangle है — एक finite patch, ना कि कुछ जो infinity तक भाग जाए।
Diagram तीनों boundary lines और उनके बीच घिरा shaded triangle दिखाता है, हर corner label के साथ।

segments_english.text: Here is the J E E Advanced version, where the work is not the graphing but deciding which constraint binds along each edge. Find the area of the region defined by x plus y at most six, x plus two y at most eight, and x and y both at least zero.
The two non-negativity conditions confine everything to the first quadrant. Now we hunt for the vertices, one edge at a time.

Start at the origin — zero-zero satisfies all four constraints, so it is a vertex. Move along the x-axis: x plus y gives x at most six, while x plus two y gives x at most eight. The tighter bound wins, so the corner is six comma zero.

Now the two slant lines. Subtract x plus y equals six from x plus two y equals eight, and the x-terms cancel, leaving y equals two. Back-substitute to get x equals four. That gives the interior vertex four comma two.
Finally, move up the y-axis: x plus y gives y at most six, while x plus two y gives y at most four. The tighter bound is four, so the corner is zero comma four.
So the feasible region is a quadrilateral, and in cyclic order the vertices are zero-zero, six-zero, four-two, and zero-four.
Apply the shoelace sum around those corners: zero, plus six times two which is twelve, plus four times four which is sixteen, plus zero — a total of twenty eight.
Halve it, and the area is one-half times twenty eight, which is fourteen square units.

<curious>And why is this Advanced-level?</curious> Not the arithmetic — it is correctly deciding which of two competing constraints clips each axis, and then assembling all four vertices in cyclic order before the shoelace step. One mis-assigned vertex throws off the whole area, as the diagram makes clear.

segments_hinglish.text: ये रहा J E E Advanced version, जहाँ काम graphing नहीं, बल्कि ये तय करना है कि हर edge पर कौन-सी constraint bind करती है। निकालो उस region का area जो x plus y at most six, x plus two y at most eight, और x और y दोनों at least zero से बना है।
दोनों non-negativity conditions सब कुछ first quadrant में समेट देती हैं। अब हम vertices ढूँढते हैं, एक-एक edge करके।

Origin से शुरू करो — zero-zero चारों constraints satisfy करता है, तो ये एक vertex है। x-axis के साथ बढ़ो — x plus y देता है x at most six, जबकि x plus two y देता है x at most eight। Tighter bound जीतता है, तो corner है six comma zero।

अब दोनों slant lines। x plus two y equals eight में से x plus y equals six घटाओ, x-terms cancel हो जाते हैं, बचता है y equals two। वापस substitute करो तो x equals four। ये देता है interior vertex four comma two।
आख़िर में, y-axis पर ऊपर बढ़ो — x plus y देता है y at most six, जबकि x plus two y देता है y at most four। Tighter bound है four, तो corner है zero comma four।
तो feasible region एक quadrilateral है, और cyclic order में vertices हैं zero-zero, six-zero, four-two, और zero-four।
उन corners के around shoelace sum लगाओ — zero, plus six times two यानी twelve, plus four times four यानी sixteen, plus zero — कुल twenty eight।
इसे आधा करो, तो area है one-half times twenty eight, यानी fourteen square units।

<curious>और ये Advanced-level क्यों है?</curious> Arithmetic नहीं — ये सही से तय करना कि दो competing constraints में से कौन हर axis को clip करती है, और फिर shoelace से पहले चारों vertices को cyclic order में जमाना। एक mis-assigned vertex पूरा area बिगाड़ देता है, जैसा diagram साफ़ दिखाता है।

title: Pitfalls and the one-point region audit

board_content.text: Where marks slip in two-variable problems
Testing (0,0) on a line through the origin. If the constant is 0, use (1,0) or (0,1).
Wrong line style: strict < > get a dotted line; $\le$ $\ge$ get a solid line.
Shading the wrong half-plane: if the test point gives 'false', shade the OPPOSITE side.
Union instead of intersection: a system needs the common overlap — only the doubly-shaded patch.
Pro-tip: pick a point clearly inside your final region and test it in EVERY inequality.
For Ex4, test $(1,1)$: $1+1=2\le6$ ✓, $1+2=3\le8$ ✓, $x,y\ge0$ ✓ — region confirmed.

segments_english.text: Let us close this subtopic with the four mistakes that quietly cost marks, and one audit that catches nearly all of them.

First and most common: testing zero-zero on a line that passes through the origin. Always glance at the constant term first. If it is zero, the line runs through the origin, so drop zero-zero and pick one-zero or zero-one instead.

Second, the wrong line style. Strict less-than and greater-than get a dotted line; the or-equal versions get a solid line. Mixing these up is the two-variable cousin of the open-versus-closed-circle error, and it costs presentation marks.
Third, shading the wrong half-plane. When your test point gives false, remember to shade the opposite side, not the side you just tested. Read your own conclusion carefully.

Fourth, union instead of intersection. A system demands that all the inequalities hold at once, so the answer is the common overlap — only the doubly, or triply, shaded patch counts. Never the combined shading.
And here is the one-point audit that protects you. After shading, pick any point clearly inside your final region and substitute it into every original inequality.

Take our shoelace example and test one comma one. One plus one is two, which is at most six. One plus two is three, which is at most eight. And both coordinates are at least zero. All three hold, so the region is confirmed — and so are your line styles.

segments_hinglish.text: इस subtopic को उन चार mistakes के साथ ख़त्म करते हैं जो चुपचाप marks खाती हैं, और एक audit जो लगभग सबको पकड़ लेता है।
पहली और सबसे common — origin से गुज़रती line पर zero-zero test करना। हमेशा पहले constant term देखो। अगर वो zero है, तो line origin से गुज़रती है, इसलिए zero-zero छोड़ो और one-zero या zero-one उठाओ।

दूसरी — ग़लत line style। Strict less-than और greater-than को dotted line मिलती है; or-equal versions को solid line। इन्हें mix करना open-versus-closed-circle error का two-variable cousin है, और ये presentation marks खाता है।
तीसरी — ग़लत half-plane shade करना। जब test point false दे, तो याद रखो कि opposite side shade करनी है, वो नहीं जो तुमने अभी test की। अपना ही conclusion ध्यान से पढ़ो।
चौथी — intersection की जगह union। System माँगता है कि सारी inequalities एक साथ hold करें, तो answer है common overlap — सिर्फ़ doubly, या triply, shaded patch गिनता है। कभी combined shading नहीं।
और ये रहा one-point audit जो तुम्हें बचाता है। Shade करने के बाद, अपने final region के अंदर कोई भी point उठाओ और उसे हर original inequality में substitute करो।

हमारा shoelace example लो और one comma one test करो। One plus one is two, जो at most six है। One plus two is three, जो at most eight है। और दोनों coordinates at least zero हैं। तीनों hold करते हैं, तो region confirm — और तुम्हारी line styles भी।

subtopic: Applications & Word Problems of Linear Inequalities
title: The hard half is translation, not solving

board_content.text: Translate → Solve → Interpret
Solving an inequality is the easy half. Turning a sentence into an inequality is the hard half.
'At least 80' means $\ge 80$ (80 allowed). 'More than 80' means $>80$. 'No more than 80' means $\le 80$.
A careless reading of the comparison word flips the entire answer.
Diwali sweet shop: cost $\le 5000$, boxes $\ge 200$, sugar $< 60$ kg. Every real constraint is an inequality.
Each leaves a whole range of legal choices — never a single number.
A quieter second skill: spotting the hidden constraints the problem never states out loud.

segments_english.text: Here is the truth about word problems: solving the inequality is the easy half. The hard half, the part that actually decides your marks, is turning a sentence of English into an inequality of mathematics.
A word problem hands you a real situation and asks for the range of possibilities. Your job has three stages — translate, then solve, then interpret back into the real world.

The single most important skill is reading the comparison words correctly. At least eighty means greater-than-or-equal to eighty, with eighty allowed. More than eighty means strictly greater than eighty, with eighty not allowed. And no more than eighty means less-than-or-equal to eighty.
These tiny distinctions matter enormously, because one careless reading of the comparison word flips the entire answer.

Picture yourself managing a sweet shop during Diwali. Every real constraint you face is an inequality, never an equation. You have at most five thousand rupees for ingredients, you must make at least two hundred boxes for pre-orders, and your storage holds under sixty kilograms of sugar.
Notice that none of these pins you to a single number. Each one leaves you a whole range of legal choices, and the art of the business is operating inside the overlap of all of them.

And there is a quieter second skill: spotting the hidden constraints the problem never states out loud. If x is the number of chairs, then x must be a whole number and cannot be negative — even though no sentence says so.

segments_hinglish.text: Word problems के बारे में सच ये है — inequality solve करना easy half है। Hard half, वो हिस्सा जो असल में तुम्हारे marks तय करता है, है English के एक sentence को mathematics की inequality में बदलना।
Word problem तुम्हें एक real situation देता है और possibilities की range माँगता है। तुम्हारा काम तीन stages में है — translate, फिर solve, फिर real world में वापस interpret।

सबसे ज़रूरी skill है comparison words को सही पढ़ना। At least eighty का मतलब greater-than-or-equal to eighty, eighty allowed। More than eighty का मतलब strictly greater than eighty, eighty allowed नहीं। और no more than eighty का मतलब less-than-or-equal to eighty।
ये छोटे-छोटे फ़र्क़ बहुत मायने रखते हैं, क्योंकि comparison word की एक careless reading पूरा answer flip कर देती है।

अपने आप को Diwali में sweet shop चलाते हुए सोचो। हर real constraint जो तुम्हारे सामने है, वो एक inequality है, equation नहीं। Ingredients के लिए तुम्हारे पास at most five thousand rupees हैं, pre-orders के लिए at least two hundred boxes बनाने हैं, और storage में under sixty kilograms sugar आती है।
देखो, इनमें से कोई भी तुम्हें single number पर नहीं बाँधता। हर एक तुम्हें legal choices की एक पूरी range देता है, और business की कला है इन सबके overlap के अंदर काम करना।

और एक quieter दूसरी skill है — वो hidden constraints पकड़ना जो problem कभी ज़ोर से नहीं कहता। अगर x chairs की संख्या है, तो x एक whole number होना चाहिए और negative नहीं हो सकता — चाहे कोई sentence ये कहे या ना कहे।

board_content.text: Rule 1: define the variable explicitly, with units — 'Let $x$ = shortest side, in cm.'
Rule 2: one condition → one inequality. Several conditions → a system, answered by intersection.
Rule 3: attach the hidden domain — $x\in\mathbb{Z},\ x\ge0$ for counts; $x>0$ for measurements.
'Between $a$ and $b$' is strict ($a<x<b$) unless the problem says 'inclusive'.

segments_english.text: The heart of this subtopic is a reliable phrase-to-symbol map, so let me put it on the board and ask you to commit it to memory.

Study the table. At least, no less than, a minimum of, not below — all mean greater-than-or-equal. At most, no more than, a maximum of, not above — all mean less-than-or-equal. More than, exceeds, over mean strictly greater; less than, under, below mean strictly less. And between a and b is a double inequality.
Now the modeling rules. Rule one: define the variable explicitly, and with units. Write, let x equal the length of the shortest side, in centimetres. A vague variable produces a vague answer.

Rule two: one condition gives one inequality. Each separate requirement in the problem becomes its own inequality, and a problem with several requirements becomes a system, whose answer is the intersection.
Rule three: attach the hidden domain. For counts, x is an integer and at least zero; for physical measurements, x is strictly greater than zero.
And a warning that trips up many: between a and b is read as strict, a less than x less than b, unless the problem explicitly says between a and b inclusive.
Finally, always state the units of your variable and carry them right through to the final answer. Units are part of a correct response, not an afterthought.

segments_hinglish.text: इस subtopic का दिल है एक reliable phrase-to-symbol map, तो चलो इसे बोर्ड पर रखता हूँ और तुमसे कहता हूँ — इसे याद कर लो।

Table देखो। At least, no less than, a minimum of, not below — सब का मतलब greater-than-or-equal। At most, no more than, a maximum of, not above — सब का मतलब less-than-or-equal। More than, exceeds, over का मतलब strictly greater; less than, under, below का मतलब strictly less। और between a and b एक double inequality है।
अब modeling rules। Rule one — variable को explicitly define करो, और units के साथ। लिखो, let x equal shortest side की length, centimetres में। Vague variable vague answer देता है।
Rule two — one condition देता है one inequality। Problem की हर अलग requirement अपनी एक inequality बनती है, और कई requirements वाली problem एक system बन जाती है, जिसका answer intersection है।
Rule three — hidden domain attach करो। Counts के लिए, x एक integer है और at least zero; physical measurements के लिए, x strictly greater than zero।
और एक warning जो कई लोगों को गिराती है — between a and b को strict पढ़ा जाता है, a less than x less than b, जब तक problem साफ़ ना कहे between a and b inclusive।
आख़िर में, हमेशा अपने variable की units बताओ और उन्हें final answer तक ले जाओ। Units सही answer का हिस्सा हैं, बाद में सोचने की चीज़ नहीं।

board_content.caption: Follow the five steps in order — that is what prevents lost marks

board_content.text: 1. Name the unknown, with units. 2. Translate each requirement into an inequality.
3. Record the hidden domain. 4. Solve — and for a system, intersect the solution sets.
5. Interpret the result in the words of the problem.
'The minimum number of boxes is 201' is what a marker rewards — not '$x\ge200$'.
Mixture setup: bound $\frac{\text{pure component}}{\text{total}}$, then clear fractions by the positive total.

segments_english.text: Word problems have no derivation — they have a disciplined routine, and following it in order is exactly what prevents lost marks. Here it is as a five-step flow.
Look at the flow on the board, top to bottom, and let me walk each box.

Step one, name the unknown, and do it with units — because every later inequality must refer to the same clearly-defined quantity. Step two, translate each requirement into an inequality, choosing the symbol deliberately from the dictionary.

Step three, record the hidden domain, whether that is x greater than zero, or x a non-negative integer. Step four, solve the inequality or the system — and for a system, take the intersection of the solution sets.
Step five, and this is the one students skip, interpret the result in the words of the problem.
A solution set is not yet an answer. The sentence a marker rewards is, the minimum number of complete boxes is two hundred one — not merely, x is at least two hundred.

One recurring setup you will meet is the mixture problem. You write the concentration as the pure component over the total amount, bound it as the problem requires, and then clear the fraction by multiplying by the total — which, being a positive quantity, never flips the inequality.

segments_hinglish.text: Word problems का कोई derivation नहीं होता — इनका एक disciplined routine होता है, और उसे order में follow करना ही lost marks रोकता है। ये रहा पाँच steps का flow।
बोर्ड पर flow देखो, ऊपर से नीचे, और मैं हर box समझाता हूँ।

Step one, unknown को name करो, और units के साथ — क्योंकि हर बाद वाली inequality उसी clearly-defined quantity को refer करनी चाहिए। Step two, हर requirement को inequality में translate करो, dictionary से symbol सोच-समझकर चुनकर।
Step three, hidden domain record करो, चाहे वो x greater than zero हो, या x एक non-negative integer। Step four, inequality या system solve करो — और system के लिए, solution sets का intersection लो।
Step five, और यही वो step है जो students छोड़ देते हैं, result को problem के शब्दों में interpret करो।
Solution set अभी answer नहीं है। जो sentence marker reward करता है वो है — minimum number of complete boxes two hundred one है — ना कि सिर्फ़, x at least two hundred।

एक बार-बार आने वाला setup है mixture problem। तुम concentration को pure component over total amount लिखते हो, उसे problem के हिसाब से bound करते हो, और फिर total से multiply करके fraction clear करते हो — जो positive quantity होने की वजह से inequality कभी flip नहीं करता।

subtopic: Applications & Word Problems of Linear Inequalities
title: The average and mixture templates

board_content.text: Two templates that cover most word problems
Average condition — 'the average of $n$ quantities is at least $A$' becomes:
Mixture condition — the concentration is the pure component over the total amount:
Bound the concentration between the target percentages, giving a double inequality in $y$.
The total $V+y>0$, so multiplying through by it to clear fractions never flips the inequality.

segments_english.text: Two templates cover the vast majority of word problems in this chapter, so let me board them as your toolkit.
First, the average condition. When a problem says the average of n quantities is at least A, you write it directly as a fraction condition.
The sum of the quantities, divided by n, is greater-than-or-equal to A. That single line captures every average-of-marks or average-of-scores problem.
Second, the mixture condition. When you blend two solutions, the concentration of the mixture is the total pure component divided by the total amount.
On the board: take V litres of an a-percent solution and add y litres of a b-percent solution; the concentration is a-over-hundred times V, plus b-over-hundred times y, all over V plus y.
You then bound that concentration between the two target percentages the problem gives, which produces a double inequality in y.

And here is the one reassurance that makes it safe: the total, V plus y, is strictly positive, so when you clear the fractions by multiplying through by it, the inequality direction never flips. That is why the mixture double-inequality solves cleanly.

segments_hinglish.text: इस chapter की ज़्यादातर word problems को दो templates cover कर लेते हैं, तो चलो इन्हें toolkit की तरह बोर्ड पर रखता हूँ।
पहला, average condition। जब problem कहे कि n quantities का average at least A है, तो तुम इसे सीधे एक fraction condition की तरह लिखते हो।
Quantities का sum, n से divided, greater-than-or-equal to A। ये एक line हर average-of-marks या average-of-scores problem को पकड़ लेती है।
दूसरा, mixture condition। जब तुम दो solutions मिलाते हो, तो mixture की concentration है total pure component, total amount से divided।
बोर्ड पर — a-percent solution के V litres लो और b-percent solution के y litres add करो; concentration है a-over-hundred times V, plus b-over-hundred times y, पूरा V plus y के ऊपर।
फिर तुम उस concentration को problem के दिए दो target percentages के बीच bound करते हो, जो y में एक double inequality बनाता है।

और ये रही वो एक बात जो इसे safe बनाती है — total, V plus y, strictly positive है, तो जब तुम इससे multiply करके fractions clear करते हो, inequality की direction कभी flip नहीं होती। इसीलिए mixture double-inequality साफ़ solve होती है।

title: Worked example: triangle perimeter (CBSE)

board_content.text: Longest side $=2\times$ shortest; third $=$ shortest $+2$; perimeter $\ge 42$
Step 1 — name: let $x$ = shortest side, in cm. Then longest $=2x$, third $=x+2$.
Step 2 — translate 'perimeter at least 42':
Step 3 — domain: $x>0$ (a length).
Step 5 — interpret: the shortest side must be at least 10 cm.
