segments_english.text: Let us run the five-step routine on a clean C B S E problem. The longest side of a triangle is twice the shortest side, the third side is two centimetres longer than the shortest, and the perimeter is at least forty two centimetres. Find the minimum length of the shortest side.
Step one, name the unknown with units. Let x be the length of the shortest side, in centimetres. Then the longest side is two x, and the third side is x plus two.
Step two, translate. Perimeter at least forty two means the sum of the three sides is greater-than-or-equal to forty two.
Writing it out: x plus two x plus the quantity x plus two, greater-than-or-equal to forty two.
Step three, the hidden domain. Since x is a length, x must be strictly greater than zero.

Step four, solve. The left side simplifies to four x plus two, so four x plus two is at least forty two. Subtract two to get four x at least forty, and divide by four — positive, no flip — to get x at least ten.
Step five, interpret in words. The shortest side must be at least ten centimetres, so its minimum length is ten centimetres. That final sentence, with its unit, is the answer a marker rewards.
The diagram shows the triangle with its three sides written in terms of the shortest side x — a useful habit for keeping the translation honest.

segments_hinglish.text: चलो एक साफ़ C B S E problem पर पाँच-step routine चलाते हैं। एक triangle की longest side shortest side की दोगुनी है, third side shortest से two centimetres लंबी है, और perimeter at least forty two centimetres है। Shortest side की minimum length निकालो।
Step one, unknown को units के साथ name करो। मान लो x, shortest side की length, centimetres में। तो longest side है two x, और third side है x plus two।
Step two, translate। Perimeter at least forty two का मतलब तीनों sides का sum greater-than-or-equal to forty two।
लिखो — x plus two x plus the quantity x plus two, greater-than-or-equal to forty two।
Step three, hidden domain। चूँकि x एक length है, x strictly greater than zero होना चाहिए।

Step four, solve। Left side simplify होकर four x plus two बनता है, तो four x plus two at least forty two। Two subtract करो, मिलता है four x at least forty, और four से divide करो — positive, कोई flip नहीं — तो x at least ten।
Step five, शब्दों में interpret। Shortest side at least ten centimetres होनी चाहिए, तो उसकी minimum length ten centimetres है। वही final sentence, unit के साथ, वो answer है जो marker reward करता है।
Diagram triangle को दिखाता है, तीनों sides shortest side x के हिसाब से लिखी हुई — translation को ईमानदार रखने की एक useful आदत।

subtopic: Applications & Word Problems of Linear Inequalities
title: Worked example: consecutive odd numbers, the hidden-domain trap

board_content.text: Consecutive odd naturals, both $>10$, whose sum $<40$
Let the smaller odd number $=x$; the next consecutive odd number $=x+2$.
'Both greater than 10': since $x$ is the smaller, $x>10$ guarantees both.
So $10 < x < 19$. Now apply the hidden domain — $x$ is an odd natural number.
$x \in \{11, 13, 15, 17\}$ — the continuous interval is NOT the answer.

segments_english.text: This is a J E E Main speed trap, and it fires on two fronts at once: the comparison words, and a hidden domain of odd integers. Find all pairs of consecutive odd natural numbers, both greater than ten, whose sum is less than forty.
Let the smaller odd number be x. Then the next consecutive odd number is x plus two.
Now, both greater than ten. Since x is the smaller of the two, simply requiring x greater than ten guarantees that both numbers clear ten.
The sum less than forty gives x plus the quantity x plus two, less than forty. That is two x plus two less than forty, so x is less than nineteen.
Combining, we have ten less than x, less than nineteen. But here is the whole point of the problem — we now apply the hidden domain: x must be an odd natural number.

The odd naturals strictly between ten and nineteen are eleven, thirteen, fifteen, and seventeen. The continuous interval is emphatically not the answer — a student who stops at ten-to-nineteen loses the marks.

So the pairs are eleven and thirteen, thirteen and fifteen, fifteen and seventeen, and seventeen and nineteen. Verify the boundary: x equals seventeen gives a sum of thirty six, which is below forty, good; but x equals nineteen would give a sum of forty, which is not less than forty, so it is correctly excluded.
The number line shows it: the open interval from ten to nineteen, with the four odd solutions marked as filled dots inside it.

segments_hinglish.text: ये एक J E E Main speed trap है, और ये एक साथ दो मोर्चों पर वार करता है — comparison words, और odd integers का एक hidden domain। Consecutive odd natural numbers के सारे pairs निकालो, दोनों greater than ten, जिनका sum less than forty हो।
मान लो smaller odd number है x। तो next consecutive odd number है x plus two।
अब, both greater than ten। चूँकि x दोनों में छोटा है, बस x greater than ten माँगना दोनों numbers को ten के ऊपर guarantee कर देता है।
Sum less than forty देता है x plus the quantity x plus two, less than forty। यानी two x plus two less than forty, तो x less than nineteen।
मिलाकर, हमारे पास है ten less than x, less than nineteen। पर यहीं है problem की पूरी बात — अब हम hidden domain लगाते हैं — x एक odd natural number होना चाहिए।
Ten और nineteen के बीच strictly odd naturals हैं eleven, thirteen, fifteen, और seventeen। Continuous interval बिलकुल answer नहीं है — जो student ten-to-nineteen पर रुक जाता है, वो marks खो देता है।

तो pairs हैं eleven और thirteen, thirteen और fifteen, fifteen और seventeen, और seventeen और nineteen। Boundary verify करो — x equals seventeen देता है sum thirty six, जो forty से नीचे है, सही; पर x equals nineteen देता sum forty, जो forty से कम नहीं, तो वो सही से excluded है।
Number line इसे दिखाता है — ten से nineteen का open interval, और उसके अंदर चारों odd solutions filled dots के रूप में।

subtopic: Applications & Word Problems of Linear Inequalities
title: Worked example: acid mixture, a rational double inequality (JEE Main)

board_content.text: 600 mL of 20% acid; add $y$ mL of 50% — result between 30% and 40%
Let $y$ = mL of the 50% solution added, with $y\ge0$.
Pure acid $= 0.20(600) + 0.50y = 120 + 0.5y$, in a total of $600+y$ mL.
Multiply throughout by the positive total $600+y$ (no flip).
Add between 300 mL and 1200 mL: $300 < y < 1200$.

segments_english.text: Now a multi-concept J E E Main problem that fuses inequalities with a percentage mixture. A chemist has six hundred millilitres of a twenty-percent acid solution. How many millilitres of a fifty-percent solution must be added so the resulting mixture is more than thirty percent but less than forty percent acid?
Let y be the millilitres of the fifty-percent solution added, with y at least zero — you cannot add a negative volume.

Now the pure-acid balance. The pure acid after mixing is zero point two zero times six hundred, plus zero point five zero times y, which is one hundred twenty plus zero point five y, sitting in a total volume of six hundred plus y millilitres.
The concentration condition is a double inequality: zero point three is less than one hundred twenty plus zero point five y, over six hundred plus y, which is less than zero point four.
Since the total, six hundred plus y, is positive, we may multiply all three parts by it with no flip.
That clears the fraction: zero point three times six hundred plus y, less than one hundred twenty plus zero point five y, less than zero point four times six hundred plus y.

Solve the two halves. The left gives sixty less than zero point two y, so y greater than three hundred. The right gives zero point one y less than one hundred twenty, so y less than one thousand two hundred.

Intersecting, three hundred less than y less than one thousand two hundred. So the chemist must add between three hundred and one thousand two hundred millilitres of the fifty-percent solution. The multi-concept move was recognising that the percentage model only becomes linear after you multiply by the positive total volume.

segments_hinglish.text: अब एक multi-concept J E E Main problem जो inequalities को percentage mixture के साथ जोड़ती है। एक chemist के पास twenty-percent acid solution के six hundred millilitres हैं। Fifty-percent solution के कितने millilitres add करने होंगे ताकि resulting mixture more than thirty percent पर less than forty percent acid हो?
मान लो y, add किए गए fifty-percent solution के millilitres, y at least zero के साथ — negative volume add नहीं कर सकते।

अब pure-acid balance। Mixing के बाद pure acid है zero point two zero times six hundred, plus zero point five zero times y, यानी one hundred twenty plus zero point five y, जो six hundred plus y millilitres के total volume में है।
Concentration condition एक double inequality है — zero point three less than one hundred twenty plus zero point five y, over six hundred plus y, less than zero point four।
चूँकि total, six hundred plus y, positive है, हम तीनों parts को इससे बिना flip multiply कर सकते हैं।
इससे fraction clear हो जाता है — zero point three times six hundred plus y, less than one hundred twenty plus zero point five y, less than zero point four times six hundred plus y।

दोनों halves solve करो। Left देता है sixty less than zero point two y, तो y greater than three hundred। Right देता है zero point one y less than one hundred twenty, तो y less than one thousand two hundred।

Intersect करने पर, three hundred less than y less than one thousand two hundred। तो chemist को fifty-percent solution के between three hundred and one thousand two hundred millilitres add करने होंगे। Multi-concept move यही था — पहचानना कि percentage model तभी linear बनता है जब तुम positive total volume से multiply करते हो।

segments_english.text: Finally, a J E E Advanced problem that is really Linear Programming in disguise — the bridge to what you will formalise in Class twelve. A small workshop makes x chairs and y tables per day.
Each chair needs two hours of carpentry and one hour of finishing; each table needs three hours of carpentry and two hours of finishing.

At most thirty six carpentry-hours and twenty two finishing-hours are available daily, and the profit is thirty rupees per chair and fifty rupees per table. We want the production plan that maximises profit.
Model the constraints. Carpentry gives two x plus three y at most thirty six; finishing gives x plus two y at most twenty two; and counts force x and y at least zero.

This system is a bounded polygon — the feasible region from the previous subtopic. Find its corner points by solving the boundary lines pairwise: the origin, eighteen-zero, zero-eleven, and the interior vertex.
That interior vertex comes from intersecting the two slant constraints, two x plus three y equals thirty six and x plus two y equals twenty two, which gives six comma eight.

Now evaluate the profit Z equals thirty x plus fifty y at each corner. At the origin, zero. At eighteen-zero, five hundred forty. At zero-eleven, five hundred fifty. And at six-eight, one hundred eighty plus four hundred, which is five hundred eighty.
So the maximum profit is five hundred eighty rupees per day, achieved at six chairs and eight tables.
The non-obvious step is recognising that the joint-constraint vertex, six-eight, beats both of the axis vertices — and the diagram shows exactly why the optimum sits at that interior corner.

segments_hinglish.text: आख़िर में, एक J E E Advanced problem जो असल में भेस बदले Linear Programming है — वो bridge जिसे तुम Class twelve में formalise करोगे। एक छोटा workshop रोज़ x chairs और y tables बनाता है।
हर chair को two hours carpentry और one hour finishing चाहिए; हर table को three hours carpentry और two hours finishing।

रोज़ at most thirty six carpentry-hours और twenty two finishing-hours available हैं, और profit है thirty rupees per chair और fifty rupees per table। हमें वो production plan चाहिए जो profit maximise करे।
Constraints model करो। Carpentry देता है two x plus three y at most thirty six; finishing देता है x plus two y at most twenty two; और counts x और y को at least zero पर मजबूर करते हैं।
ये system एक bounded polygon है — पिछले subtopic वाला feasible region। इसके corner points boundary lines को pairwise solve करके निकालो — origin, eighteen-zero, zero-eleven, और interior vertex।
वो interior vertex दोनों slant constraints को intersect करने से आता है, two x plus three y equals thirty six और x plus two y equals twenty two, जो देता है six comma eight।

अब हर corner पर profit Z equals thirty x plus fifty y evaluate करो। Origin पर, zero। Eighteen-zero पर, five hundred forty। Zero-eleven पर, five hundred fifty। और six-eight पर, one hundred eighty plus four hundred, यानी five hundred eighty।
तो maximum profit है five hundred eighty rupees per day, six chairs और eight tables पर।
Non-obvious step यही है — पहचानना कि joint-constraint vertex, six-eight, दोनों axis vertices को हरा देता है — और diagram ठीक-ठीक दिखाता है कि optimum उस interior corner पर क्यों बैठता है।

subtopic: Applications & Word Problems of Linear Inequalities
title: Pitfalls and the translate-then-test habit

board_content.text: Where word problems leak marks
Misreading the comparison word: 'more than' is strict >; 'at least' is inclusive $\ge$.
Underline the phrase and write its symbol BEFORE building the inequality.
Forgetting the hidden domain: a count is a non-negative integer; a length is positive.
Stopping at '$x\ge10$' instead of 'the minimum length is 10 cm' — always interpret back.
Mishandling 'between': treat it as strict unless the problem says 'inclusive'.
Pro-tip: after forming the inequality, plug a valid scenario back in to confirm the symbols.
For Ex1, test $x=10$: perimeter $=10+20+12=42\ge42$ ✓ — 'at least' correctly read as $\ge$.

segments_english.text: Let us close the subtopic with the mistakes that quietly cost marks on word problems, and one habit that catches almost all of them.

First and most common: misreading the comparison word. More than is strict greater-than; at least is inclusive greater-than-or-equal. These are not interchangeable, and confusing them flips the boundary.
So build a physical habit — underline the comparison phrase in the question and write its symbol down before you build the inequality. Decide the symbol deliberately, not reflexively.
Second, forgetting the hidden domain. A count is a non-negative integer; a length is strictly positive. Solve over the reals first, then restrict — and state the restricted answer.

Third, stopping at x greater-than-or-equal to ten instead of the minimum length is ten centimetres. A bare solution set is not a sentence a marker rewards — always interpret back into the words of the problem.
Fourth, mishandling between. Treat it as strict unless the problem explicitly says inclusive. Many students reflexively write the or-equal version and lose the endpoint.
And here is the habit that saves you: after forming the inequality, plug a clearly-valid scenario from the problem back in, to confirm your symbols point the right way.

For our triangle example, test x equals ten. The perimeter is ten plus twenty plus twelve, which is forty two, and forty two is at least forty two — true. That confirms the boundary is included and that at least was correctly read as greater-than-or-equal.

segments_hinglish.text: चलो subtopic को उन mistakes के साथ ख़त्म करते हैं जो word problems में चुपचाप marks खाती हैं, और एक habit जो लगभग सबको पकड़ लेती है।

पहली और सबसे common — comparison word ग़लत पढ़ना। More than strict greater-than है; at least inclusive greater-than-or-equal है। ये interchangeable नहीं हैं, और इन्हें confuse करना boundary flip कर देता है।
तो एक physical habit बनाओ — question में comparison phrase underline करो और inequality बनाने से पहले उसका symbol लिख लो। Symbol सोच-समझकर तय करो, reflexively नहीं।
दूसरी — hidden domain भूलना। Count एक non-negative integer है; length strictly positive। पहले reals पर solve करो, फिर restrict करो — और restricted answer बताओ।

तीसरी — x greater-than-or-equal to ten पर रुक जाना, बजाय ये कहने के कि minimum length ten centimetres है। एक सूखा solution set वो sentence नहीं जो marker reward करता है — हमेशा problem के शब्दों में वापस interpret करो।
चौथी — between को ग़लत handle करना। इसे strict मानो जब तक problem साफ़ ना कहे inclusive। कई students reflexively or-equal version लिख देते हैं और endpoint खो देते हैं।
और ये रही वो habit जो तुम्हें बचाती है — inequality बनाने के बाद, problem से एक clearly-valid scenario वापस डालो, ये confirm करने के लिए कि तुम्हारे symbols सही तरफ़ इशारा कर रहे हैं।

हमारे triangle example के लिए, x equals ten test करो। Perimeter है ten plus twenty plus twelve, यानी forty two, और forty two at least forty two है — true। ये confirm करता है कि boundary included है और at least सही से greater-than-or-equal पढ़ा गया।

title: When one sign-flip is no longer enough

board_content.text: Beyond linear: products, squares, quotients
Linear was easy: $ax+b$ changes sign exactly once, so a single flip rule handled everything.
You cannot solve $x^2>4$ by 'square-rooting', nor $\frac{x-1}{x+2}\ge0$ by cross-multiplying.
The key fact: a continuous expression can only switch sign by passing through zero.
Mark every zero (and every blow-up point); those critical points chop the line into intervals.
Inside each interval the sign is CONSTANT — find it once, then propagate across the rest.
Walking left→right along $(x-1)(x-3)(x+2)$: each root crossed flips one factor, so the product flips.
Odd powers CROSS the axis; even powers TOUCH and BOUNCE. That multiplicity rule is the whole game.

segments_english.text: Linear inequalities had one comforting feature: the expression a x plus b changes sign exactly once, so a single flip rule handled everything. The moment the expression becomes non-linear — a product, a square, a quotient — that simplicity ends.
Say that again to yourself: for linear, one flip was enough, because the sign changed only once.

But you cannot solve x squared greater than four by simply square-rooting both sides, and you cannot solve x minus one over x plus two, greater-than-or-equal to zero, by cross-multiplying — because the sign of what you multiply by is unknown. A completely different, and rather beautiful, idea is needed.
That idea rests on one fact: a continuous expression can only switch between positive and negative by passing through zero.
So if you mark on the number line every point where the expression equals zero — or blows up to infinity — those critical points chop the line into intervals.

And inside each interval the sign stays constant. That means you determine the sign in just one interval and then let a simple rule propagate it across all the rest. This is the method of intervals, and its visual form is the wavy curve.

Picture walking left to right along a product like x minus one, times x minus three, times x plus two. Far to the right every factor is positive, so the product is positive. Now walk leftward — each time you cross a root, one factor flips sign, so the whole product flips.

But there is a crucial exception. Odd powers cross the axis; even powers merely touch it and bounce back to the same side. That single rule about multiplicity is what separates a correct J E E solution from a wrong one.

segments_hinglish.text: Linear inequalities का एक comforting feature था — expression a x plus b का sign ठीक एक बार बदलता है, तो एक ही flip rule सब कुछ संभाल लेता था। जिस पल expression non-linear बनता है — एक product, एक square, एक quotient — वो simplicity ख़त्म।
अपने आप को दोहराओ — linear के लिए एक flip काफ़ी था, क्योंकि sign सिर्फ़ एक बार बदलता था।

पर तुम x squared greater than four को दोनों sides का square root लेकर solve नहीं कर सकते, और x minus one over x plus two, greater-than-or-equal to zero, को cross-multiply करके नहीं — क्योंकि जिससे multiply कर रहे हो उसका sign पता नहीं। एक बिलकुल अलग, और काफ़ी ख़ूबसूरत, idea चाहिए।
वो idea एक fact पर टिका है — एक continuous expression positive और negative के बीच सिर्फ़ zero से गुज़रकर switch कर सकता है।
तो अगर तुम number line पर हर वो point mark करो जहाँ expression zero है — या infinity तक उछलता है — वो critical points line को intervals में काट देते हैं।

और हर interval के अंदर sign constant रहता है। यानी तुम सिर्फ़ एक interval में sign determine करते हो और फिर एक simple rule उसे बाक़ी सबमें propagate कर देता है। यही है method of intervals, और इसका visual रूप है wavy curve।

एक product के साथ left to right चलने की कल्पना करो, जैसे x minus one, times x minus three, times x plus two। दाईं तरफ़ दूर हर factor positive है, तो product positive। अब बाईं तरफ़ चलो — हर बार जब एक root cross करते हो, एक factor sign flip करता है, तो पूरा product flip हो जाता है।
पर एक crucial exception है। Odd powers axis को cross करती हैं; even powers बस उसे touch करके उसी side पर bounce हो जाती हैं। Multiplicity का वही एक rule एक सही J E E solution को ग़लत से अलग करता है।

title: The factor, endpoint, and multiplicity rules

board_content.text: The rules that keep the method honest
Write every factor as $(x-r)$ with a POSITIVE coefficient on $x$.
So $(3-x)$ must become $-(x-3)$ — and track that stray minus sign.
Even-multiplicity roots (squared, ...) are touch-and-bounce: the sign does NOT flip there.
Denominator zeros are critical points too — but the expression is undefined there.
Denominator roots are ALWAYS open circles, regardless of $\le$ or $\ge$.
A numerator root may be included only for a non-strict ($\le$, $\ge$) inequality.

segments_english.text: Before we compute anything, four rules keep the wavy-curve method honest. Get these wrong and every interval after them inverts.
First, write every factor in the standard shape x minus r, with a positive coefficient on x. The crossing-and-bouncing rule is stated for that shape, so it must match.

That means a factor like three minus x must be rewritten as minus the quantity x minus three — and you must track that stray minus sign, because a hidden negative silently inverts every sign in your answer.
Second, and this is the star rule: even-multiplicity roots — squared, fourth-power, and so on — are touch-and-bounce points. The sign does not flip as you pass them.
Third, denominator zeros are critical points too, since the expression can change sign around them — but the expression is undefined at a denominator zero.
So denominator roots are always open circles — hollow — regardless of whether the inequality is less-than-or-equal or greater-than-or-equal. They can never be part of the solution.

Fourth, a numerator root may be included only for a non-strict inequality. Under a strict less-than or greater-than, even numerator roots are excluded, because there the expression equals zero, not something strictly positive or negative.

segments_hinglish.text: कुछ भी compute करने से पहले, चार rules wavy-curve method को honest रखते हैं। इन्हें ग़लत करो और उनके बाद का हर interval उल्टा हो जाता है।
पहला, हर factor को standard shape x minus r में लिखो, x पर positive coefficient के साथ। Crossing-and-bouncing rule उसी shape के लिए कहा गया है, तो match होना चाहिए।

इसका मतलब three minus x जैसे factor को minus the quantity x minus three लिखना पड़ेगा — और उस stray minus sign को track करना ज़रूरी है, क्योंकि एक छिपा negative तुम्हारे answer के हर sign को चुपचाप उल्टा कर देता है।
दूसरा, और यही star rule है — even-multiplicity roots — squared, fourth-power, वग़ैरह — touch-and-bounce points हैं। इनसे गुज़रते वक़्त sign flip नहीं होता।
तीसरा, denominator zeros भी critical points हैं, क्योंकि expression उनके around sign बदल सकता है — पर denominator zero पर expression undefined होता है।
तो denominator roots हमेशा open circles होते हैं — hollow — चाहे inequality less-than-or-equal हो या greater-than-or-equal। ये कभी solution का हिस्सा नहीं हो सकते।

चौथा, एक numerator root सिर्फ़ non-strict inequality के लिए included हो सकता है। Strict less-than या greater-than के तहत, numerator roots भी excluded हैं, क्योंकि वहाँ expression zero के बराबर होता है, strictly positive या negative नहीं।

title: The wavy-curve algorithm, step by step

board_content.text: Six steps for any polynomial or rational inequality
1. Move everything to one side so the other side is 0.
2. Combine into one quotient and factor completely into $(x-r)$; make each $x$-coefficient positive.
3. Mark critical points: numerator zeros (filled if $\le/\ge$, hollow if strict); denominator zeros (always hollow).
4. Fix the rightmost sign: for very large $x$ all factors are positive, so start ABOVE the axis on the far right.
5. Draw leftward: CROSS at odd-multiplicity roots, TOUCH and BOUNCE at even ones.
6. Read the intervals on the required side, then adjust the endpoints.
Quadratic 'outside vs between' falls right out: $a(x-\alpha)(x-\beta)$ is + outside, − between.

segments_english.text: Now the algorithm itself — six steps that solve any polynomial or rational inequality. Learn the order and the traps disappear.
Step one: move everything to one side so the other side is exactly zero. The method reads the sign of a single expression against zero, so comparing two non-zero sides is meaningless.
Step two: combine into one quotient and factor completely into linear factors x minus r, and irreducible quadratics which keep a constant sign — then make each x-coefficient positive.
Step three: mark all critical points. Numerator zeros are filled if the inequality is non-strict and hollow if strict; denominator zeros are always hollow, because they are forbidden values.

Step four: fix the rightmost sign. For x larger than every critical point, all positive-coefficient factors are positive, so the expression is positive there — start the wavy curve above the axis on the far right.
Step five: draw the curve leftward, obeying multiplicity. Cross the axis at odd-multiplicity roots, touch and bounce at even-multiplicity roots.

Step six: read off the intervals where the curve lies on the required side — above for greater-than-zero, below for less-than-zero — then adjust the endpoints, including numerator roots for non-strict inequalities and excluding all denominator roots.

And notice a gift. The quadratic outside-versus-between rule falls right out of this. A quadratic with positive leading coefficient factors as a, times x minus alpha, times x minus beta — positive outside the roots, negative between them. It is just a one-line wavy curve.

segments_hinglish.text: अब algorithm ख़ुद — छह steps जो किसी भी polynomial या rational inequality को solve करते हैं। Order सीख लो और traps ग़ायब हो जाते हैं।
Step one — सब कुछ एक side ले जाओ ताकि दूसरी side बिलकुल zero हो। Method एक single expression का sign zero के ख़िलाफ़ पढ़ता है, तो दो non-zero sides को compare करना meaningless है।
Step two — एक quotient में combine करो और completely linear factors x minus r में factor करो, और irreducible quadratics में जो constant sign रखती हैं — फिर हर x-coefficient positive बनाओ।
Step three — सारे critical points mark करो। Numerator zeros filled अगर inequality non-strict है और hollow अगर strict; denominator zeros हमेशा hollow, क्योंकि वो forbidden values हैं।

Step four — rightmost sign fix करो। हर critical point से बड़े x के लिए, सारे positive-coefficient factors positive हैं, तो expression वहाँ positive है — wavy curve को far right पर axis के ऊपर से शुरू करो।
Step five — curve को बाईं तरफ़ draw करो, multiplicity मानते हुए। Odd-multiplicity roots पर axis cross करो, even-multiplicity roots पर touch करके bounce करो।

Step six — वो intervals पढ़ो जहाँ curve required side पर है — greater-than-zero के लिए ऊपर, less-than-zero के लिए नीचे — फिर endpoints adjust करो, non-strict inequalities के लिए numerator roots include करके और सारे denominator roots exclude करके।

और एक gift देखो। Quadratic का outside-versus-between rule इसी से निकल आता है। Positive leading coefficient वाला quadratic factor होता है a, times x minus alpha, times x minus beta — roots के बाहर positive, बीच में negative। ये बस एक one-line wavy curve है।

title: Standard results: modulus and quadratic

board_content.text: Results to memorise (a > 0)

board_content.latex: x^2 < a^2 \iff |x| < a, \qquad x^2 > a^2 \iff |x| > a

board_content.text: Quadratic $ax^2+bx+c$ with $a>0$ and real roots $\alpha<\beta$:
No real roots and $a>0$ ⇒ the expression is positive for ALL $x$.

segments_english.text: A handful of standard results are worth memorising outright, because they let you skip the full wavy curve on the common cases. Assume a is positive throughout.
The modulus, less-than form: the modulus of x is less than a exactly when x lies between negative a and a. Less-than traps you inside a single interval.
The modulus, greater-than form: the modulus of x is greater than a exactly when x is less than negative a, or x is greater than a. Greater-than throws you outside, into a union of two pieces.

The squared forms are useful because squares are sign-free: x squared less than a squared is the same as modulus x less than a, and x squared greater than a squared is the same as modulus x greater than a.
Now the quadratic, with positive leading coefficient a and real roots alpha less than beta.
The quadratic is negative exactly between the roots — alpha less than x less than beta.
And the quadratic is positive exactly outside the roots — x less than alpha, or x greater than beta.
One more, easy to forget: if the discriminant is negative so there are no real roots, and a is positive, the parabola sits entirely above the axis, so the expression is positive for every single x.

segments_hinglish.text: कुछ standard results सीधे याद करने लायक़ हैं, क्योंकि ये common cases पर पूरा wavy curve skip करा देते हैं। पूरे समय a positive मानो।
Modulus, less-than form — modulus of x less than a ठीक तब जब x negative a और a के बीच हो। Less-than तुम्हें एक single interval के अंदर फँसा देता है।
Modulus, greater-than form — modulus of x greater than a ठीक तब जब x less than negative a, या x greater than a। Greater-than तुम्हें बाहर फेंक देता है, दो टुकड़ों के union में।
Squared forms useful हैं क्योंकि squares sign-free होते हैं — x squared less than a squared वही है जो modulus x less than a, और x squared greater than a squared वही है जो modulus x greater than a।
अब quadratic, positive leading coefficient a और real roots alpha less than beta के साथ।
Quadratic negative है ठीक roots के बीच — alpha less than x less than beta।
और quadratic positive है ठीक roots के बाहर — x less than alpha, या x greater than beta।
एक और, भूलना आसान — अगर discriminant negative है यानी कोई real roots नहीं, और a positive है, तो parabola पूरी axis के ऊपर बैठता है, तो expression हर एक x के लिए positive है।

title: Worked example: a quadratic inequality (foundational)

board_content.text: Solve $x^2 - x - 6 > 0$
Factor the quadratic.
Roots are $x=-2$ and $x=3$, and the coefficient of $x^2$ is positive.
'$>0$' means OUTSIDE the roots (a positive-leading parabola is positive outside).
Both endpoints excluded — the inequality is strict.

board_content.caption: Parabola positive (shaded) outside the roots -2 and 3

segments_english.text: Let us start with a foundational quadratic to see the standard result in action. Solve x squared minus x minus six, greater than zero.
First, factor the quadratic.
It factors as x minus three, times x plus two.
So the roots are x equals negative two and x equals three, and importantly, the coefficient of x squared is positive, so this is an upward parabola.
The inequality is greater than zero, and a positive-leading parabola is positive outside its roots. So we want the outside region.
That gives x less than negative two, or x greater than three — in interval form, negative infinity to negative two, union three to infinity.
Both endpoints are excluded, because the inequality is strict.

The diagram shows the upward parabola crossing the axis at negative two and three, dipping below between them and rising above on both outer sides — and those two outer stretches, where the curve is above the axis, are exactly the shaded solution.

segments_hinglish.text: एक foundational quadratic से शुरू करते हैं ताकि standard result को action में देखें। Solve करो x squared minus x minus six, greater than zero।
पहले, quadratic को factor करो।
ये factor होता है x minus three, times x plus two।
तो roots हैं x equals negative two और x equals three, और ज़रूरी बात — x squared का coefficient positive है, तो ये एक upward parabola है।
Inequality greater than zero है, और positive-leading parabola अपने roots के बाहर positive होता है। तो हमें outside region चाहिए।
इससे मिलता है x less than negative two, या x greater than three — interval form में, negative infinity से negative two, union three से infinity।
दोनों endpoints excluded हैं, क्योंकि inequality strict है।

Diagram upward parabola दिखाता है, negative two और three पर axis cross करते हुए, बीच में नीचे डुबकी और दोनों बाहरी sides पर ऊपर उठते हुए — और वही दो बाहरी हिस्से, जहाँ curve axis के ऊपर है, बिलकुल shaded solution हैं।

title: Worked example: modulus inequality, the direction trap

board_content.text: Solve $|2x - 3| \ge 5$
'$\ge$' throws you OUTSIDE into a union — the opposite of the '$\le$' form.
Apply $|f|\ge a \iff f\le -a$ or $f\ge a$:
Endpoints included — the inequality is non-strict.

board_content.caption: Filled at -1 and 4; shaded outward (a union of two rays)

segments_english.text: This is a J E E Main speed trap built entirely on modulus direction. Solve the modulus of two x minus three, greater-than-or-equal to five.

Here is the trap. The greater-than-or-equal form throws you outside, into a union of two intervals — the exact opposite of the less-than form. A student who writes negative five less-than-or-equal to two x minus three less-than-or-equal to five, the less-than template, gets precisely the wrong region.
Apply the correct rule: modulus of f greater-than-or-equal to a means f less-than-or-equal to negative a, or f greater-than-or-equal to a.
So two x minus three is at most negative five, or two x minus three is at least five.
Solve each. The left gives two x at most negative two, so x at most negative one. The right gives two x at least eight, so x at least four.
So the solution is the union: negative infinity to negative one, closed, together with four to infinity, closed.
Both endpoints are included, because the inequality is non-strict.
The number line shows it perfectly — filled dots at negative one and four, with the shading running outward from each, a union of two rays with a gap in the middle.

segments_hinglish.text: ये एक J E E Main speed trap है जो पूरी तरह modulus direction पर बना है। Solve करो modulus of two x minus three, greater-than-or-equal to five।

यहाँ है trap। Greater-than-or-equal form तुम्हें बाहर फेंकता है, दो intervals के union में — less-than form का बिलकुल उल्टा। जो student negative five less-than-or-equal to two x minus three less-than-or-equal to five लिखता है, यानी less-than template, वो बिलकुल ग़लत region पाता है।
सही rule लगाओ — modulus of f greater-than-or-equal to a का मतलब f less-than-or-equal to negative a, या f greater-than-or-equal to a।
तो two x minus three at most negative five, या two x minus three at least five।
हर एक solve करो। Left देता है two x at most negative two, तो x at most negative one। Right देता है two x at least eight, तो x at least four।
तो solution है union — negative infinity से negative one, closed, साथ में four से infinity, closed।
दोनों endpoints included हैं, क्योंकि inequality non-strict है।
Number line इसे perfectly दिखाता है — negative one और four पर filled dots, हर से बाहर की तरफ़ shading, बीच में gap के साथ दो rays का union।

title: Worked example: a rational inequality, the safe route

board_content.text: Solve $\dfrac{x-4}{x+1} < 1$
Do NOT cross-multiply — the sign of $x+1$ is unknown.
Bring everything to one side instead, and combine into one fraction.
The numerator $-5$ is a negative constant, so the fraction is negative exactly when $x+1>0$.
$x=-1$ excluded — the original expression is undefined there.

segments_english.text: Now a rational inequality, and the single most common error students make on it. Solve x minus four, over x plus one, less than one.

Here is what you must not do: do not cross-multiply by x plus one. Its sign is unknown, so you cannot tell whether to flip the inequality. Cross-multiplying is exactly how rational inequalities break beginners.
The safe route is to bring everything to one side and combine into a single fraction.

Subtract one: x minus four over x plus one, minus one, is less than zero. Put over the common denominator: the quantity x minus four, minus the quantity x plus one, all over x plus one — and the numerator simplifies beautifully to just negative five over x plus one, less than zero.
Now read it. The numerator, negative five, is a fixed negative constant. A negative divided by something is negative exactly when that something is positive — so we need x plus one greater than zero.
That gives x greater than negative one — the interval negative one to infinity.

And note x equals negative one is excluded, because the original expression is undefined there. The lesson is simple: bringing everything to one side and combining is the safe route every single time.

segments_hinglish.text: अब एक rational inequality, और इस पर students की सबसे common error। Solve करो x minus four, over x plus one, less than one।

ये है जो तुम्हें नहीं करना — x plus one से cross-multiply मत करो। इसका sign पता नहीं, तो flip करना है या नहीं ये तय नहीं कर सकते। Cross-multiplying ही वो तरीक़ा है जिससे rational inequalities beginners को तोड़ देती हैं।
Safe route है सब कुछ एक side लाना और एक single fraction में combine करना।

One subtract करो — x minus four over x plus one, minus one, less than zero। Common denominator पर लाओ — the quantity x minus four, minus the quantity x plus one, पूरा x plus one के ऊपर — और numerator ख़ूबसूरती से simplify होकर बस negative five over x plus one, less than zero बन जाता है।
अब पढ़ो। Numerator, negative five, एक fixed negative constant है। एक negative किसी चीज़ से divided negative तभी होता है जब वो चीज़ positive हो — तो हमें x plus one greater than zero चाहिए।
इससे मिलता है x greater than negative one — interval negative one से infinity।
और ध्यान दो, x equals negative one excluded है, क्योंकि original expression वहाँ undefined है। Lesson simple है — सब कुछ एक side लाकर combine करना हर बार safe route है।

title: Worked example: the full wavy curve (JEE Advanced)

board_content.text: Critical points L→R: $-3$ (num, mult 1), $-2$ (denom), $1$ (num, mult 2), $4$ (num, mult 1).
Anchor: for large $x$ all factors are positive ⇒ start POSITIVE on the far right.
Walk left: cross at $4$ (odd) → −; bounce at $1$ (even) → stays −; cross at $-2$ → +; cross at $-3$ → −.
We need '$\ge 0$' — the curve on or above the axis.
Include $-3$ and $4$ (numerator roots); exclude $-2$ (denominator); keep the isolated $\{1\}$.

segments_english.text: Now the full J E E Advanced showpiece, where three traps fire at once. Solve the quantity x plus three, times x minus one squared, times x minus four, all over x plus two, greater-than-or-equal to zero.

List the critical points left to right. Negative three is a numerator root of multiplicity one. Negative two is a denominator root. One is a numerator root of multiplicity two. And four is a numerator root of multiplicity one.
Now anchor the sign. For x larger than every critical point, every factor is positive, so the whole expression is positive — start the wavy curve above the axis on the far right.

Walk leftward. Cross at four, an odd root, so the sign turns negative on one to four. Reach one, an even root, so we bounce — the sign stays negative through negative two to one. Cross at negative two, the denominator root, so it turns positive on negative three to negative two. And cross at negative three, so it turns negative on the far left.
So the sign pattern is: negative, then positive, then negative, negative, and finally positive on the far right.
We need greater-than-or-equal to zero — so we collect the intervals where the curve is on or above the axis.

The positive stretch negative three to negative two: include negative three, a numerator root under a non-strict inequality, but exclude negative two, a denominator root. And the point x equals one makes the numerator zero, so under greater-than-or-equal it survives as an isolated solution — keep the single point one. And the positive stretch four to infinity: include four.
So the answer is negative three to negative two, closed then open, union the single point one, union four to infinity closed.

The wavy curve on the board makes all three traps visible at once — the bounce at the squared root one, the open exclusion of the denominator root negative two, and the inclusion of the simple numerator roots. Miss any one and the answer is wrong.

अब sign anchor करो। हर critical point से बड़े x के लिए, हर factor positive है, तो पूरा expression positive — wavy curve को far right पर axis के ऊपर से शुरू करो।

बाईं तरफ़ चलो। Four पर cross, एक odd root, तो sign one से four पर negative हो जाता है। One पर पहुँचो, एक even root, तो bounce — sign negative two से one तक negative ही रहता है। Negative two पर cross, denominator root, तो negative three से negative two पर positive। और negative three पर cross, तो far left पर negative।

तो answer है negative three से negative two, closed फिर open, union single point one, union four से infinity closed।

title: The four wavy-curve traps

board_content.text: Where non-linear inequalities go wrong
Cross-multiplying a rational inequality by a variable denominator — its sign is unknown.
Always bring to one side and combine into a single quotient first.
Wrong modulus direction: $|f|<a$ locks you INSIDE; $|f|>a$ throws you OUTSIDE into a union.
Including a denominator zero: never in the solution — an open circle always, even under $\le/\ge$.
Forgetting the even-multiplicity bounce: at a squared root the sign does NOT flip.
Pro-tip: fix the far-right sign as positive, then walk left — flip at odd roots, bounce at even.

segments_english.text: Let us close the subtopic — and the whole chapter's teaching — with the four traps that sink non-linear inequalities, and the pro-tip that anchors everything.
First and deadliest: cross-multiplying a rational inequality by a variable denominator. Its sign is unknown, so you cannot know whether to flip. This is the top rational-inequality mistake.
The cure is always the same: bring everything to one side and combine into a single quotient before you do anything else.

Second, wrong modulus direction. Modulus of f less than a locks you inside a single interval; modulus of f greater than a throws you outside, into a union of two. Mixing these up inverts your whole answer.

Third, including a denominator zero. A value that makes the denominator zero is never in the solution — it is an open circle always, even under a non-strict less-than-or-equal or greater-than-or-equal.

Fourth, forgetting the even-multiplicity bounce. At a squared, or any even-power, root, the curve touches and returns; the sign does not flip. Treating it as a normal crossing inverts half your intervals.

And the pro-tip that ties it together: after making all x-coefficients positive, anchor the wavy curve as positive on the far-right interval, then walk left — flipping at odd roots and bouncing at even ones. One test substitution at a large x confirms the anchor before you propagate.

segments_hinglish.text: चलो subtopic — और पूरे chapter की teaching — को उन चार traps के साथ ख़त्म करते हैं जो non-linear inequalities को डुबो देते हैं, और वो pro-tip जो सब कुछ anchor करता है।
पहला और सबसे घातक — rational inequality को variable denominator से cross-multiply करना। इसका sign पता नहीं, तो flip करना है या नहीं ये पता नहीं चल सकता। ये top rational-inequality mistake है।
इलाज हमेशा एक ही है — कुछ भी और करने से पहले सब कुछ एक side लाओ और एक single quotient में combine करो।

दूसरा, ग़लत modulus direction। Modulus of f less than a तुम्हें एक single interval के अंदर lock कर देता है; modulus of f greater than a तुम्हें बाहर फेंक देता है, दो के union में। इन्हें mix करना पूरा answer उल्टा कर देता है।
तीसरा, denominator zero को include करना। जो value denominator को zero बनाए, वो कभी solution में नहीं — हमेशा एक open circle, non-strict less-than-or-equal या greater-than-or-equal के तहत भी।
चौथा, even-multiplicity bounce भूलना। एक squared, या किसी भी even-power, root पर, curve touch करके लौट आता है; sign flip नहीं होता। इसे normal crossing मानना तुम्हारे आधे intervals उल्टे कर देता है।

और वो pro-tip जो सब बाँधता है — सारे x-coefficients positive बनाने के बाद, wavy curve को far-right interval पर positive anchor करो, फिर बाईं तरफ़ चलो — odd roots पर flip और even पर bounce करते हुए। एक बड़े x पर एक test substitution propagate करने से पहले anchor confirm कर देता है।

title: The complete inequalities toolkit

board_content.text: Every formula from the chapter, on one board
Endpoints: numerator roots in for $\le/\ge$; denominator roots always out; $\infty$ always round.

segments_english.text: Before the final quick-recall, here is your complete toolkit — every formula from the whole chapter consolidated onto one board. I am restating these, not re-teaching them, so treat this as your one-page reference.
The engine of the whole chapter: if a is less than b and c is negative, then c a is greater than c b. The negative flips the sign. Everything else follows from this.
The general linear inequality: a x plus b greater than zero gives x greater than negative b over a when a is positive, and the flipped version when a is negative.
Two variables: the boundary a x plus b y equals c is plotted from its intercepts, c over a comma zero, and zero comma c over b.
And for the area of a bounded region, the shoelace formula — one-half the absolute value of the cyclic sum of x-i y-i-plus-one minus x-i-plus-one y-i.
The two word-problem templates: the average condition, sum over n at least A; and the mixture condition, pure component over total amount.
The modulus results: modulus x less than a traps you inside, between negative a and a; modulus x greater than a throws you outside, into a union.
The quadratic, with positive leading coefficient: negative between the roots, positive outside them.

And the endpoint rule that governs them all: numerator roots are included for non-strict inequalities, denominator roots are always excluded, and infinity always takes a round bracket. That is the entire chapter on one board.

title: Quick recall for the whole chapter

board_content.text: Linear Inequalities — quick recall
One variable: the solution is a range. Add/subtract and multiply-by-positive are safe; multiply-by-negative flips.
'Negative flips, positive sticks.' — 'Infinity never gets a hug (square bracket).'
Two variables: a line splits the plane; $\le\ge$ solid, <> dotted; test (0,0) unless the line runs through it; system ⇒ intersection.
Word problems: read the word, then write the sign; counts are whole & non-negative; interpret back — don't stop at '$x\ge10$'.
Wavy curve: one side $=0$, factor with positive $x$-coeffs, anchor + on far right, odd cross / even bounce.
'Odd crosses, even bounces.' — 'Denominators get a hole, never a dot.'

segments_english.text: And now the one-screen cheat sheet for the whole chapter — six ideas and their mnemonics, everything you need in the last minute before the exam.
One variable: the solution is always a range, so answer in interval form. Adding, subtracting, and multiplying by a positive are safe; multiplying or dividing by a negative flips the sign.
The mnemonics to lock it in: negative flips, positive sticks; and, infinity never gets a hug — meaning infinity always takes a round bracket, never a square one.

Two variables: a line splits the plane into half-planes. Less-than-or-equal and greater-than-or-equal draw solid, strict signs draw dotted. Test the origin unless the line runs through it, and for a system, take the intersection.

Word problems: read the comparison word first, then write the sign. A count is a whole, non-negative number. And always interpret back — do not stop at x greater-than-or-equal to ten; say what it means.
The wavy curve: move everything to one side equal to zero, factor with positive x-coefficients, anchor the sign as positive on the far right, then cross at odd roots and bounce at even ones.
Its mnemonics: odd crosses, even bounces; and, denominators get a hole, never a dot — a denominator root is always an open circle.
Modulus in one line: less-than locks you in, to a single interval; greater-than lets you out, into a union of two.

And the quadratic with positive leading coefficient: negative between the roots, positive outside them; and if there are no real roots, it is positive for every x. That is the whole chapter, ready for revision.
